EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sat, 07 Nov 2026 08:50:38 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 ‘A photograph allows us to really stare’: new Brussels exhibition documents modern human slavery, ahead of EU Parliament debate https://euobserver.com/247592/a-photograph-allows-us-to-really-stare-new-brussels-exhibition-documents-modern-human-slavery-ahead-of-eu-parliament-debate/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247592 A Brussels photography exhibition on modern slavery opened this week, exposing the cruelty of contemporary human-trafficking, often against women and girls, ahead of MEP discussions on the EU's new strategy.]]> A new photography exhibition examining modern slavery opened this week in Brussels – ahead of European Parliament discussions on fresh strategies against such human trafficking.

In the Nepalese mountains, a woman comes back to her village with jewellry and shining trinkets, giving the appearance of wealth. She promises local kids jobs in Kathmandu.

“The whole village supports the kids going…. What they didn’t know is she was trafficked,” Lisa Kristine, an American photographer profiling human trafficking victims, told EUobserver.

The “Slavery: Stories of the Present” exhibition opened on Thursday (5 November) in Géopolis, a city-supported photo-journalism museum in Brussels.

It features works of two photographers focusing on modern slavery around the world and on women and girls in rural Afghanistan, often forced to marry in their early teens.

About 50 million people were enslaved as of 2022, with some 27 million in forced labour, and 22 million married against their will, according to the International Labour Organisation data. The number grew by 10 million since 2016.

Many are sold off to pay for family debts, others are lured with false promises of good job conditions. 

Read more

‘Younger and younger victims’: EU faces challenge of AI-fuelled online sex trafficking

In the EU alone, at least 880,000 people are forced to work, including 270,000 being sex-trafficked.

Photography, argues Kristine, one of the two photographers whose works make up the exhibition, is a good method of raising awareness on the topic: contrary to statistics or even an eye-to-eye encounter, “a photograph allows for us to really stare.” This way, the viewer can take the time to see the other person and open up to empathy.

“The issue is rather abstract, full of data… but when you actually see a human being, it speaks more to your heart,” Kristine told EUobserver.

Pictures by the other photographer, Élise Blanchard, show Afghan girls and women, whose families have often lost their herding grounds or could no longer farm on their land as a result of climate change. Selling their daughters for marriage is a way out of family debts.

“I’m not trying to frighten somebody or overwhelm somebody with something horrific…” she said, highlighting the human dignity she tries to show through her portraits.

]]> Italy still obstructing asylum returns from other EU states amid simmering dispute that threatens Schengen https://euobserver.com/247568/italy-still-obstructing-asylum-returns-from-other-eu-states-amid-simmering-dispute-that-threatens-schengen/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:21:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247568 Italy's foot-dragging on taking back asylum seekers from other EU states is contributing to a simmering dispute that risks shattering whatever trust has been restored among member states on the Schengen border-free travel zone.]]> Rome is still not fully accepting the return of prospective asylum seekers from countries such as Germany even though they first entered Europe on Italian territory, in a simmering dispute that could potentially erupt and place further pressure on the EU’s border-free travel zone.

A document released on Friday (6 November) by the European Commission says transfer requests were still being rejected as of the end of September.

“Based on the information provided by the member states between 12 June and 30 September 2026, transfers requested by other member states continued to be rejected by the Italian authorities,” says the document.

“Furthermore, according to information received, there have been cases in which the Italian authorities returned persons to the transferring member states, despite Italy having been determined as the member state responsible,” it added.

Even though it says Italy, as of 29 October, has resumed transfers, according to an administrative letter, the European Commission couldn’t determine if anyone had actually departed for Italy.

The findings highlight a politically-explosive scenario whereby arriving asylum seekers fan out through the rest of Europe, triggering knee-jerk reactions by member states to impose internal border controls on the Schengen area.

It also echoes the scenario whereby Italy slapped border controls on Spain over the summer over unfounded fears that the tens of thousands of people that entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta would somehow end up on continental Europe.

Italy has for years allowed people to leave without first registering them, in a process of self-relocation that has angered other EU states. Many travel through France to reach northern Europe.

]]> Trump vows ‘beautiful’ Russia deal, as EU agonises over which envoy to send to Ukraine peace talks https://euobserver.com/247519/trump-vows-beautiful-russia-deal-as-eu-agonises-over-which-envoy-to-send-to-ukraine-peace-talks/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:11:19 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247519 Discussions on the EU envoy will take place at an informal summit in Dublin on 13 November, after Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni bewailed the current "disarray" of various European diplomatic formats on the war.]]> EU leaders are to discuss who should speak for them in potential high-level Ukraine peace talks, but some commentators do not believe Russia is interested in any “big, beautiful” deal.

The internal EU discussion will take place at an informal summit in Dublin on 13 November, following an exchange of letters between EU Council president António Costa and Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who bewailed the current “disarray” of various European diplomatic formats on the war.

The Dublin meeting will focus on the “profile, format, and mandate” of the job, leaving till later proposals on individual names, an EU source said.

Meloni told Costa that “I am not asking for this role for myself or for Italy”, but did not rule herself out either.

]]> EU prosecutors launch possible €110m fraud probe into Spain’s railways, after second lethal crash https://euobserver.com/247457/eu-prosecutors-launch-possible-e110m-fraud-probe-into-spains-railways-after-second-lethal-crash/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:06:21 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247457 Spain is under investigation for its spending of €110m in EU development funds granted for planned renovation of the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line, following a second deadly accident on the high-speed line in 2026.]]> The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) on Friday (6 November) launched an investigation into the Spanish state railway for possible fraud of EU funds for maintenance of the line that saw a second deadly collision this year on 28 October.

The EU’s independent prosecutor in Madrid launched the probe into the use of European funds following the crash on the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line that killed 69 people in Toledo last week, while an earlier accident in January left a further 46 dead on the same route. 

The EPPO’s headquarters in Luxembourg announced they launched investigative measures into Spain’s Administrator of Railway Infrastructure (ADIF), its State Railway Safety Agency (AESF) and the Court of Auditors in Spain. 

The European Commission stayed silent on the procedures when asked at a press briefing on Friday, since EPPO procedures are launched independently of EU institutions.

Read more

Two fatal train disasters in less than a year: I never thought I would see this happen in my native Spain

Agents of the Civil Guard visited both offices on Friday morning, to request documents that may show any evidence of embezzlement of European funds in the maintenance works of the high-speed rail line.

]]> Russians repel attack by Ukrainian ground-robots armed with RPGs, in futuristic assault (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,716) https://euobserver.com/247493/russians-repel-attack-by-ukrainian-ground-robots-armed-with-rpgs-in-futuristic-assault-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1716/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:29:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247493 Ukrainian commander Andriy Biletsky is gambling on mass robot assaults to spare his soldiers’ lives, as Russian troops rush to prove on camera that they can still swat the machines from the sky and fields around Lyman. ]]>
  • Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps is saving lives by sending robots into attacks.
  • In Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka, Russians are being pushed out of built-up areas.
  • Even after more than half a year, Z-patriots cannot fully admit defeat in Dnipropetrovsk region, but fear the situation in Komar.
  • The death toll from the attack on Komyshuvakha has risen to 53.
  • Kyiv has been plunged into darkness, without water or sewage services — Russia is attacking more intensely, and the capital was unprepared.
  • The effectiveness of shooting down drones is improving very slowly.
  • Maps of the day — Orikhiv. Velyka Novosilka direction.
  • Videos of the day — what the failed ground-drone attack looked like from the Russian perspective; Kyiv without electricity; a MiG-29 shot down a drone with its cannon at point-blank range; a Geran-5 crashed into a field; a new type of interceptor drone.

    • Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps sent dozens of robots into an attack. This was the same formation that carried out the successful Vivaldi operation near Lyman.

    During that operation, the corps had already used various innovative methods of deploying drones. Among other things, heavy aircraft transported armed ground drones deep behind Russian lines, catching Russian defences by surprise.

    Now, units under the command of Andriy Biletsky tried another innovation. So far, the course and outcome of the fighting are known only from Russian sources. Other information may emerge over time, but for now the attempt can be considered unsuccessful.

    Nevertheless, it is an extraordinary example of how an army suffering from a manpower shortage and seeking to protect its limited resources uses modern technology. It also suggests how drones could help break the deadlock at the front and shift from static to mobile warfare.

    The Russians claim that as many as 28 drones attacked without the direct involvement of a single Ukrainian soldier in combat.

    The Russian Telegram channel Military Informant counted two drones armed with US-made Mk 19 grenade launchers, 18 drones equipped with two RPGs each, and eight kamikaze drones loaded with explosives among those involved in the attack.

    At the third attempt in a matter of weeks, member states backed the Irish council presidency’s compromise, which keeps the commission’s proposed one-year delay timeline. 

    Read more

    [Investigation] How the EU’s methane rules came undone, and ended up giving Trump exactly what he wanted

    Importers would have to start monitoring, reporting and verifying the methane emissions of the oil and gas they buy abroad from 1 January 2028 instead of January 2027.

    Reporting on the methane intensity of imported oil, gas and coal would be postponed to 5 August 2029, and maximum intensity limits would apply from 5 August 2031, one year later than planned.

    But the compromise also asks the EU Commission to assess whether importers are actually able to comply with the rules, before 30 September next year.

    ]]>         From India to Africa, renewables race ahead but Europe is lagging, IEA report shows https://euobserver.com/247441/from-india-to-africa-renewables-race-ahead-but-europe-is-lagging-iea-report-shows/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:05:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247441 The Iran war has pushed governments from India to sub-Saharan Africa to build more solar and wind, with some regions almost tripling new capacity. But in Europe, that rollout is stalling. ]]> The oil and gas shock from the Strait of Hormuz is speeding up the transition to renewables almost everywhere in the world, but not in Europe, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its annual renewables report on Friday (6 November).

    The Paris-based agency expects global renewable power capacity to grow by almost 4,800 GW between 2026 and 2031, which is 57 percent more than in the previous six years. 

    But it cut its expected growth forecast for Europe by six percent compared to estimates made last year, although Europe will still add around 100 gigawatts (GW) a year until 2031.

    “Higher electricity prices associated with the current conflict in the Middle East have not yet translated into major policy revisions or a measurable acceleration in installations,” the report says about the situation in Europe. 

    In most places, the adoption of renewables is speeding up, driven by high costs of fuels and energy security worries. 

    “Previously, environmental concerns were the policy priority behind the growth of renewables,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol on Friday. 

    “Today, it’s mainly energy security that is driving renewables’ expansion as more and more countries seek to reduce their exposure to imported fuels,” he also said. 

    The IEA raised its forecast for the United States by almost 40 percent compared with last year, and for sub-Saharan Africa by 54 percent.

    For the first time, poorer countries outside China will add renewables as fast as rich ones.

    ]]>         Hungary’s communist secret‑police files go online – and a Fidesz MP is named by mistake (Day 178 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/247289/hungarys-communist-secretpolice-files-go-online-and-a-fidesz-mp-is-named-by-mistake-day-178-of-the-tisza-government/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:42:10 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247289 Budapest finally opens its communist-era files and trims money for cultural and diaspora projects. Prime minister Péter Magyar navigates a minefield where each disclosure risks empowering Fidesz loyalists and unsettling Hungary’s neighbours alike. ]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Secret-police files: familiar names and an embarrassing error.
    • Director of the Institute of International Affairs dismissed – he had also worked for the Fidesz government.
    • Government causes major uproar with cultural budget.
    • Less money may go across the borders.
    • Poll of the week: a majority wants slower, but lawful and effective justice.

    Sándor Lezsák was one of the founders of the Hungarian party called MDF at the time of the country’s regime change from communism; it was in the yard of his house in Lakitelek where the meetings preparing the transition took place, where opposition politicians held discussions in the late 1980s.

    Lezsák later became a Fidesz politician and served as a MEP for the party until the 2026 election. His name also appeared in the state security documents published on Wednesday (4 November), which he immediately and vehemently protested against.

    “Everyone who spreads this vile lie will be held accountable for it in court,” he wrote.

    It soon emerged that his name indeed should not have appeared in the files.

    On Thursday morning the Historical Archives of the State Security Services announced that Lezsák’s name had appeared on the website due to an IT error. In reality he was not a network contact, but a person under surveillance.

    Fidesz politicians immediately seized on the case.

    “Tisza, in truly neo-communist fashion, is lumping perpetrators together with victims,” reacted parliamentary group leader János Bóka, demanding an apology from prime minister Péter Magyar and the resignation of cultural minister Zoltán Tarr.

    Magyar later publicly apologised to Lezsák.

    A belated step

    On 15 September the Hungarian parliament decided to make public, and searchable online, the list of people who cooperated with the communist secret services (the so‑called “network contacts”).

    In the first phase, part of the documents was made accessible on the site nyitottaktak.hu, while the recruitment dossiers – from which the stories of those recruited can be learned in more detail – will be published by 25 February 2027, the Memorial Day for the Victims of the Communist Dictatorship.

    Hungary is thus taking this step 37 years after the regime change, more than 20 years after the Czech Republic and Slovakia did so in 2004.

    Those we already knew about

    It was already known in the case of several well‑known public figures that they had cooperated with the secret services or had come into their sights.

    One such person was Nobel Prize‑winning biologist Katalin Karikó, developer of Pfizer’s vaccines, about whom it emerged in 2021 that state security had recruited her. At the time Karikó said she had been recruited under threat, but had not reported on anyone.

    It had also long been known that other politicians had been recruited: among them József Torgyán, former president of the Independent Smallholders’ Party, who in 1998 was Viktor Orbán’s coalition partner, and István Csurka, who led the far‑right party called MIÉP.

    The files also contain the name of György Nógrádi, one of Fidesz’s best‑known geopolitics experts, who often appears in Slovakia and was previously a guest at MKP (the party of the Hungarians living in Slovakia) campaign events. Nógrádi denies having been an agent.

    New names appear too

    On Wednesday (4 November) the whole of Hungary was feverishly browsing the site nyitottaktak.hu to see which familiar names might surface.

    There were indeed some surprises.

    By Thursday the lists had produced the names of several television personalities, singers, artists and other public figures. One of the best‑known is István Vágó, who for decades hosted popular quiz shows and was regarded as one of the most erudite figures on Hungarian television.

    The list also includes Tibor Dévényi, one of the first Hungarian DJs, who for decades hosted the popular children’s programme Three Wishes on public television. The Fidesz‑adjacent singer Róbert Szikora is likewise among the well‑known names; he has denied having ever reported on anyone.

    Among those on the list there is a sitting Constitutional Court judge (András Patyi), a former ambassador to Washington (András Simonyi), and even a former central bank governor (György Surányi).

    ]]>         Listen: The mental health toll of Europe’s migration policies https://euobserver.com/247374/listen-the-mental-health-toll-of-europes-migration-policies/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:38:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247374 Racism, violence, institutional abandonment and unbearable living conditions.  These are all factors that damage the mental health of migrants and exiled people. That’s exactly what migrants in Ceuta are experiencing since July.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Racism, violence, institutional abandonment and unbearable living conditions.  These are all factors that damage the mental health of migrants and exiled people. That’s exactly what migrants in Ceuta are experiencing since July. 

    Does the EU really care about migrants’ mental health? The conditions in which they often find themselves in Europe create stress, anxiety and a lack of hope. These have very concrete effects on their psychological state.

    Léa has been working in Ceuta since July as a volunteer for the non profit organisation No Name Kitchen, that supports migrants and refugees. In an interview with our partner inside the Sphera network, El Salto, she speaks about the migrants she has met so far. Her name has been changed:

    “In these months I have seen the change in the boys’ faces. As the weeks passed they transformed. It was them, but it wasn’t them anymore.”

    Read more

    Afghan pushback survivor fights ‘impossible’ evidence rules in European courts with new UN case against Greece

    When journalist Sarah Babiker from El Salto spoke to those who are closest to the migrants in Ceuta, she noticed that they all describe a climate of intense tension and speak about a mental health crisis.

    Léa is observing systematic violence on the city streets: “I didn’t find a single person who hadn’t had experiences of violence or racism with security forces or neighbors.” In this context, she says, more and more people are asking for care for mental health problems. Some do not request it explicitly, but would actually need it.

    Migrating is an obstacle course that takes a toll not only on bodies but also on mental health. Léa stresses that every phase of migration is traumatic: before crossing the border, during the crossing, and also on arrival. Migrants are experiencing wars, sometimes death and distress.

    As a result, they are more likely to develop post-traumatic stress, depression and anxiety. On top of this, there is the case of people who already had mental health problems beforehand and can no longer be followed up or treated correctly. 

    So how do authorities take that into account? Let’s be clear: access to psychosocial care is very limited in the support provided to migrants.

    Legislation varies from one EU member state to another, because there is no common European legislation on mental health care for new arrivals. 

    Read more

    Merz, Meloni and the EU: How political attacks on rescue charities are leaving migrants to drown

    What happens is that the measures in place often apply only to those with refugee status. There is often no care at all while people wait for a decision on their case. This takes months, if not years.

    What’s more, the language barrier and the fear of being deported often make it harder for people to speak openly and ask for help. In Ceuta, healthcare centres, or workers, are often difficult to access because of harassment from security forces, neighbours or, sometimes, the far-right. 

    For example, Léa recalls that one time when taking migrants to Médecins du Monde, they were forced to stop and get out of the car. The migrants believed for a few minutes that they were going to be deported. She describes how they were subjected to racist remarks, while the authorities refused to call Médecins du Monde to check that they were indeed heading there, preferring to arrest them.

    That’s why taking care of mental health cannot go without recognising the most basic human rights.

    Read more

    ‘Let me die’: tortured migrants and rescue ships face off against EU-sponsored Libyan forces

    The problem is that politics seems to go in the opposite direction: Several NGOs and mental health organizations have already pointed out that tighter border controls, temporary reception facilities and, more broadly, the hardening of migration policies risk worsening psychosocial distress. They also make it even harder to identify vulnerable people with mental health problems.

    So what do we do about it? In Sweden, Red Cross trauma centres treat refugees whatever their papers say, with interpreters in the room. In Ireland, a charity offers free counselling with no documents needed, and they insist that nothing is shared with immigration. In Germany, no less than fifty centres help survivors of torture, war and forced displacement.

    Those places care for everyone in their own language, without fear, factors that are essential to supporting migrants’ mental health.

    One last word to conclude: the struggle migrants face surely complicates their integration. But more importantly: this struggle doesn’t disappear when their status is cleared. 

    Even when allowed to stay legally on the territory, they face racism and discrimination, further poisoning their integration and thus feeding the far right discourse.

    ]]>         After students voted out Vučić, can Serbia’s uprising against ‘evil’ change how the state really works? https://euobserver.com/247121/after-students-voted-out-vucic-can-serbias-uprising-against-evil-change-how-the-state-really-works/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:05:11 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247121 The student movement's triumph over Aleksandar Vučić has built an unprecedented pro-democracy political momentum in Serbia. Their win follows two years of government crackdowns on protests kick-started by the Novi Sad railway station disaster two years ago.]]> It is evening a few days after the Serbian election, and young people have gathered in central Belgrade.

    The group has laid out paints and brushes on the pavement. Until a few days ago, the building had been graffitied with insults towards student protesters.

    A young woman writes a student protest slogan on the wall in Serbian: “Love is in the streets.” It is one of the slogans that accompanied the student protests.

    “We are trying to turn the city into a kind of gallery,” explained 17-year-old student protester Adam.

    On 30 September, the US department of war announced an Autonomous Warfare Command, meant to scale autonomous warfare across the US military by October 2027.

    Others, such as professor Elke Schwarz from the Queen Mary University of London, have long shown how the commercial logic of technology firms shapes the ethics of violent technologies, treating moral and legal questions as engineering problems to be optimised away.

    From a technical and legal perspective, this is neither possible nor desirable. Project Meridian promises that this logic will set the agenda.

    The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence fell from 40 staff to nine in 2025, and the Pentagon’s own inspector general concluded the department no longer has the personnel and capabilities needed to meet its legal responsibilities.

    Organisations like Airwars, which document civilian harm from military operations, find themselves offering evidence to commands that have almost no one left to receive it, let alone learn lessons to improve practices over time. 

    Autonomy and AI-enabled targeting depend on high quality data and feedback. A system is only as good as what its operators learn from its errors.

    Research on the quantification logics of targeting, and on outdated intelligence feeding strike decisions, shows how easily speed and scale displace the judgment that precautions require.

    Accelerating autonomy while abandoning the ability to learn from past practices does not produce a more precise or legitimate military.

    European standards for testing and assurance, limiting civilian harm written into procurement contracts, and legal review that begins at the design stage would give governments real choices about what they buy and on what terms.

    Any supplier, American or European, would have to meet them. 

    In Geneva, European governments should back the start of negotiations on a legal instrument, and they should write responsibility by design into their own procurement now, without waiting for a treaty.

    Europe should demand a different theory of responsibility from whoever supplies its autonomy.

    ]]>

      <title>Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/07/democrats-economy-affordability-crisis</link>
      <description><p>There’s not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over prices</p><p>It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.</p><p>Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/07/democrats-economy-affordability-crisis">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october</link>
      <description><p>‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December</p><p>The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.</p><p>Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/usemployment">unemployment rate</a> went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy</link>
      <description><p>Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/nov/05/what-happens-after-the-blue-wave-our-reporters-answer-your-midterm-election-results-questions">Q&amp;A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.</p><p>Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/07/cost-of-living-poll-groceries-gas">affordability crisis</a>, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">believed</a> the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/05/tech-barons-america-musk-bezos-zuckerberg</link>
      <description><p>Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult</p><p>The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.</p><p>The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/05/tech-barons-america-musk-bezos-zuckerberg">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires</link>
      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1011492107">proposed that</a> rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.</p><p>They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 08 Nov 2026 06:29:59 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[The magnificent one: Apple is winning by sitting out the AI spending race]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/08/the-magnificent-one-apple-is-winning-by-sitting-out-the-ai-spending-race/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/08/the-magnificent-one-apple-is-winning-by-sitting-out-the-ai-spending-race/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:18:00 +0000Forget the magnificent seven. Apple has become the magnificent one.

Up over 25 per cent in 2026, the iPhone maker is back on top of the stock market, with a valuation of $5 trillion putting it ahead of Nvidia.

Creative Planning strategist Charlie Bilello recently noted Apple was the only magnificent seven stock to outperform the S&P 500 this year.

The contrast with 2025 is striking. “AI is turning Apple into a market ‘loser’”, headlined Axios in July 2025, a message echoed by Bloomberg (“Apple faces calls to reboot AI strategy with shares slumping”).

Criticised for spending too little on AI, Apple now benefits as investors fret about how much its rivals are spending. Apple generates more free cash flow than any other magnificent seven member, while avoiding the AI spending binge “draining” its peers, says Bilello.

Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent a combined $202 billion on capital expenditure in the third quarter alone, more than double the year-earlier figure. Concerns over Alphabet’s cash burn sent its shares down 19 per cent in October, their worst-ever monthly performance.

Apple, which reported earnings on Monday, has essentially become a hedge against the AI trade, outperforming the Nasdaq-100 by almost 20 percentage points over the past six months.

Given its recent run, with shares up 25 per cent since June and $1 trillion added to its market value, Apple has arguably done well simply to hold on to those gains amid the recent market turbulence.

Ironically, the flight to safety has not come cheap. Apple trades at 36 times expected earnings, almost twice the S&P 500 multiple. Apple’s AI issues remain, but its reluctance to spend heavily is looking less foolish as the bills mount up elsewhere.

]]>Frederic J. Brown<![CDATA[Effects of Unite case being quietly felt in courts two years on]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/effects-of-unite-case-being-quietly-felt-in-courts-two-years-on/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/effects-of-unite-case-being-quietly-felt-in-courts-two-years-on/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000It’s not only the unions that talk about the waves made by the Supreme Court’s decision in Unite’s case against HA O’Neill a couple of years back. Legal experts are talking about them too.

Last week, at an Irish Congress of Trade Unions event, former chair of the Labour Court Kevin Duffy argued that Chief Justice Donal O’Donnell’s observation in his judgment on the case that “the right to form unions would be of little benefit if the activities of the union and its members were to be regarded as presumptively unlawful” might have the effect of undermining the Government’s claim that it cannot legislate to require employers to engage in collective bargaining in certain circumstances due to constitutional issues.

It is, Duffy suggested, simply a question of political will.

On Friday, Cathy Maguire SC pointed to another of the judgments in the case, that of Judge Brian Murray, as having hinted at the possibility of a right to strike being recognised at some point in the future.

“It is arguably implicit in Article 40.6.1 iii of the Constitution that the right to form trade unions implies in turn at least some – perhaps as yet undefined – zone of freedom for those unions to organise and campaign,” he wrote.

The observation, Maguire made clear, did not do anything to actually recognise such a right but, she said, Murray “raised the question” that it (the constitutional right of freedom of association) “may in the future be held to encompass a right to strike”.

The more immediate benefit to unions already appears to be evidenced in the absence, since the court delivered its decision two years ago, of cases taken by employers seeking injunctions intended to thwart strike action.

The court’s “definitive interpretation” had the effect of “correcting the almost universal approach”, she said, to considering such applications under the existing legislation, sections of which “should be read to give effect to the protection of unions and their members which the Acts were clearly intended to provide,” wrote O’Donnell

With employers having apparently concluded they are less likely to get injunctions, they appear to have more or less abandoned the tactic and, said Maguire, “it appears the court’s intention that these matters be played out on the picket line and not in the Four Courts has been fulfilled”.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[More than 100 Irish start-ups head to Web Summit alongside largest-ever Chinese delegation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/more-than-100-irish-start-ups-head-to-web-summit-alongside-largest-ever-chinese-delegation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/more-than-100-irish-start-ups-head-to-web-summit-alongside-largest-ever-chinese-delegation/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Travelling to Lisbon to attend Web Summit next week are 115 Irish start-up businesses – ranging from a healthtech firm that uses artificial intelligence to reduce medical appointment no-shows to a climate-conscious company that decarbonises factory operations.

They will exhibit their business ideas to some of the 70,000 people estimated to attend the technology conference throughout the week and pitch to potential investors to help fund their ideas.

Led by chief executive Paddy Cosgrave, Web Summit’s main technology conference was held in Dublin until 2015, when it was then moved to Lisbon. The events company now runs similar Web Summit conferences in Vancouver, Rio de Janeiro and Doha.

This year’s Lisbon Web Summit features its largest-ever Chinese delegation. “Their presence comes as China’s AI models gain ground globally, challenging US technological leadership and raising questions about Europe’s competitiveness,” the company said in a statement.

With the number of Irish start-ups exhibiting at the event this year representing a 36 per cent increase from 2025, Web Summit said “the record turnout comes as Irish start-ups face a challenging fundraising environment” at home and abroad.

Venture capital funding into Irish-owned small and medium-sized businesses fell by 10 per cent in the first half of this year, down to €578 million, according to research conducted by the Irish Venture Capital Association (IVCA).

International financiers accounted for 82 per cent of all investment during that period, IVCA said, representing “flashing red warning signals” for the sector.

“Irish founders have the ambition to build businesses that matter far beyond our shores,” said Richard Forde, vice president of global ecosystems at Web Summit.

“We want more founders to see global growth as a possibility from day one. Ireland can be the starting point for ideas that change industries, solve problems and create lasting value around the world,” he said.

The company has established the Irish Startup Network to bring 36 start-ups from Ireland to attend Web Summit free of charge and connect with investors and entrepreneurs.

Tickets to attend the tech event range from €1,595 for general admission to €1,950 for VIP access and €24,950 for a “chairperson” ticket – typically marketed towards company executives with additional access to the conference’s leading speakers.

Among the featured Irish start-ups is Spryt, a Monaghan-based health and wellness company that uses AI agents to “help healthcare providers reduce no – shows, improve patient engagement and make access to care easier” through automated, AI-powered WhatsApp and text messages to patients.

Climeaction, a Cork-born engineering firm founded in 2021 that reduces companies’ carbon emissions and operational costs through specialised energy audits, will also head to the conference next week, as will ClubSport, a Cavan-based software development company that has partnered with more than 600 sports clubs to manage their digital services.

]]>Patricia De Melo Moreira<![CDATA[Primark must convince investors that its best days aren’t over]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/07/primark-must-convince-investors-that-its-best-days-arent-over/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/07/primark-must-convince-investors-that-its-best-days-arent-over/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:23:00 +0000Most analysts agree the planned separation of Primark (known as Penneys in Ireland) from Associated British Foods (ABF) makes sense.

Primark has become a major international retailer in its own right, and the consensus has long been that separating it from ABF’s food businesses could help ease the so-called conglomerate discount that can weigh on valuations.

However, while ABF shares have advanced slightly since April’s demerger announcement, they have nevertheless slipped some 6 per cent in 2026, and the company’s latest results show Primark faces a challenge in convincing investors that its best days are not behind it.

Primark sales rose 2 per cent to £4.7 billion in the first half, but like-for-like sales fell 2.7 per cent. The UK delivered modest growth with a 1.3 per cent increase, but continental Europe was much weaker, with sales from established stores falling 5.6 per cent.

New stores contributed 4 per cent to overall sales growth, underlining the importance of expansion, but the performance of existing stores is harder to disguise.

Panmure Liberum said it remained “cautious on the pace of Primark’s turnaround”, identifying a recovery in like-for-like sales as central to the investment case.

On a conference call with analysts, Primark chief executive and Dubliner Eoin Tonge spoke about reinvigorating the customer proposition, with renewed emphasis on value, improvements to the womenswear range and increased marketing and digital investment.

Aer Lingus profits slump as airline plans capacity and job cuts

However, these initiatives come at a cost, with operating margins falling to 10.1 per cent. Few investors question the logic of the demerger, due by December 2027, but separating Primark from ABF will not, in itself, solve its trading problems.

]]>Dara Mac Dónaill<![CDATA[Tesco looks to open shop at Comans pub in Rathgar village]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/tesco-looks-to-open-shop-at-comans-pub-in-rathgar-village/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/tesco-looks-to-open-shop-at-comans-pub-in-rathgar-village/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000British supermarket group Tesco is poised to open a shop at the former Comans pub in Rathgar village, which has been shut for many years following a dispute within the family owners.

It is understood that Tesco is in advanced negotiations to acquire the site, which has a large car park at the rear.

A deal is yet to be signed off but if an agreement is reached, Tesco will move to secure permission for a change of use from planners to open a store in the building of the pub.

A number of other bidders are believed to have expressed an interest in the property.

Tesco is expected to retain the exterior to maintain the heritage of the building, which is located on Terenure Road East and is opposite a SuperValu shop owned by Musgrave.

The retailer already has stores in nearby Terenure and Rathmines villages, and an outlet in Rathgar would boost its presence in this affluent part of south Dublin.

No comment was available from Tesco.

The pub was opened in the late 1950s by Patrick Coman and his wife Mary. The family traded from there for almost half a century until a legal dispute arose with their sons and it has been shut for many years.

The family also owned the pub next door, called Bottlers Bank, which was a former bank branch and continues to trade.

In 2022, Agar Commercial Property sought offers in excess of €1.25 million for the car park behind the pub, which was said to have potential for the development of 18 apartments. No deal for the site was secured.

The family also operated a wholesale drinks business, which was merged with a Heineken subsidiary in 2016.

Tesco to open four new Irish stores as expansion continues

The site originally contained a grocery store with a small pub at the front. There was also previously a restaurant operating above the restaurant.

Tesco’s Irish operation increased its pretax profits last year by 8.6 per cent to €211.6 million, latest accounts show.

The retailer has 194 outlets in the Republic at present, with another four due to open by the end of 2026. This means it is set to open its 200th Irish store early in the new year.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[SW3 Capital’s Irish arm books €11.2m profit after investment sale]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/sw3-capitals-irish-arm-books-112m-profit-after-investment-sale/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/sw3-capitals-irish-arm-books-112m-profit-after-investment-sale/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000An Irish company controlled by low-profile Irish property investors behind London-based SW3 Capital booked a profit of more than €11 million last year.

SW3 Capital, controlled by Adam Rooney, Tom O’Mahony and Ned Truman, has been involved in a number of large Irish property projects and deals, including the Exo Building in Dublin’s docklands, in the past decade.

New financial filings by SW3 Capital Ireco Limited show the firm swung from a €37,985 loss to an €11.2 million profit last year.

The property investment firm said the profit was linked to the disposal of investments in 2025. It did not specify what investments were disposed of during the year.

At the end of 2025, the Irish investment company, which also received €370,000 of dividend income during the year, booked net assets of almost €11.9 million and was sitting on accumulated profits of €11.9 million.

The Irish subsidiary is ultimately owned by SW3 Capital Limited, a UK-incorporated company based in London. Rooney, O’Mahony and Truman each hold an equal stake in the parent firm, which has no single controlling party.

Before setting up SW3 Capital in 2012, Truman and O’Mahony cofounded London-based property investment business Hiberno Saxon in 2009, while Rooney previously worked for Nomura International and Rand Merchant Bank in London.

The company raised funds to invest across all sectors within the Irish market.

By 2015, it managed €110 million of assets following deals for Dublin Business School on Aungier Street; the Department of Justice’s HQ on St Stephen’s Green, Twilfit House at the junction of Jervis Street and Upper Abbey Street, Tesco Express on College Green and a mixed-use block at the corner of Dawson Street and St Stephen’s Green.

In 2016, the firm established a joint venture with Tristan Capital Partners to acquire rental sector assets in Ireland. The following year, it acquired about 400 rental units in Dublin and part-funded works on the Exo Building in Dublin’s docklands, which was the city’s tallest office block when completed.

SW3 Capital was selected by German property group DWS in 2019 as its operating partner in Dublin’s residential real estate sector.

In 2020, SW3 Capital and Tristan Capital sold a 385-home rental portfolio called Project Vert for €215 million. That same year, the fund was part of three transactions to acquire 800 homes with a gross development value of €410 million.

The following year, the firm established a joint venture with BlackRock Inc and acquired a 300-unit rental scheme in Clay Farm, Leopardstown, Dublin 18, for €125 million.

Rooney, O’Mahony and Truman’s residential management platform Occu, set up in 2019, is SW3’s residential management platform that manages rental homes on behalf of partners such as DWS.

Occu has expanded to operate across 27 Dublin locations, with more than 4,500 units under management. It recently made its first move into the UK market.

In recent months, SW3 Capital also announced the launch of a new asset management business called Gofer Hospitality. The firm has partnered with UK-based investor and developer Firethorn Trust to deliver its first hostel development on Sackville Place in Dublin, which is scheduled to open in the first quarter of next year.

]]><![CDATA[Virgin Media Ireland records €72.9m loss as it sets aside €4m for company restructuring]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/virgin-broadband-suffers-72m-loss-as-it-sets-aside-4m-for-company-restructuring/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/07/virgin-broadband-suffers-72m-loss-as-it-sets-aside-4m-for-company-restructuring/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000The broadband and mobile services offshoot of Virgin Media has set aside nearly €4 million to allow for “restructuring costs”, its newly-filed financial accounts reveal, as the business suffered a loss of more than €72 million last year.

]]><![CDATA[Ireland’s towns offer part of the solution to the housing crisis. We should seize it now]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/07/irelands-towns-offer-part-of-the-solution-to-the-housing-crisis-we-should-seize-it-now/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/07/irelands-towns-offer-part-of-the-solution-to-the-housing-crisis-we-should-seize-it-now/Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Mass dereliction and vacancy blights almost all Irish market towns. You’ve seen it for yourself: once bustling commercial centres are lifeless, hollowed out by dilapidation and urban neglect. As shopping places, most towns are barely hanging on and the more we insist that ground floors be reserved for retail space, the more widespread the sense of abandonment will become. The future of shops is not the main street, but that doesn’t mean the main street has no future, it just has one that looks different.

Shopping in the 21st century is not like shopping in the 20th or 19th centuries when most of our market towns were built. According to Eurostat, 96 per cent of Irish internet users made online purchases in 2024, the highest share in the European Union. We are rejecting the idea of the local town as a retail destination but people still want to live, socialise and hang out in towns. Is there a way to achieve this and the attendant footfall, without forcing all ground floors to be shops? What about abandoning the notion that shops should be at street level?

This week, the State nudged its way towards this by announcing a new plan that will encourage businesses to move into vacant shopfronts in towns. Rolled out across 26 designated town centres, the initiative will target empty retail properties. Rather than shops, the new plan envisages that businesses or services might move in instead. Welcome as this is, it is not enough and probably has more to do with the fact that business rates pay a chunk of county council revenue, which councils want more than innovative new town planning.

A small town in Co Kerry and a formula for rejuvenating rural Ireland

Most towns in Europe were originally derived from medieval constructs, built around commercial fairs where farmers bought and sold their produce. Around such markets, basic urban life, with artisans, money lenders, churches and taverns eventually developed. Commerce was geographically centred – the town was the locus of commerce. Urban evolution was determined by commerce. As agricultural productivity grew and fewer workers were required on the land, the urban population expanded. If you were an artisan and lived in an urban environment, your existence and life experience were quite distinct from that of your ancestors, farm labourers on the land who were beholden to some hereditary knight or feudal baron. In the town you were more free, leading to the German expression “stadtluft macht frei” (“urban air makes you free”). Floating in the air of the city were radical ideas of individual sovereignty, encouraging for the dissenter or outsider. The word ‘bourgeois’ comes from these newly commercial people who lived in the ‘burgh’ or the town.

Of course, the economic history of towns and small cities predates medieval times. For example, the Greek empire was made up of many dozens of free, self-governing city states. To organise this new type of society, a new idea emerged: the polis. By the sixth century BC, the polis – or the town – was firmly established as the foundation of all Greek civilisation. Obviously the word politics derives from it. The polis was the civic, social, economic, military and political cornerstone of ancient Greece and the rules of the polis outlined citizens’ rights and obligations. The Greek polis was organised around the agora, the marketplace, a space not just for the exchange of goods but for ideas and sedition too.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[The man who lobbies for Ireland’s hotels: ‘A lounge boy today could be general manager in 20 years’ time on €250K’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/hotels-lobbying-chief-paul-gallagher-our-lobbying-was-behind-doors-not-on-radio/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/hotels-lobbying-chief-paul-gallagher-our-lobbying-was-behind-doors-not-on-radio/Fri, 06 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000“You could be the lounge boy today and be the general manager in 20 years time on a quarter of a million euros,” says Paul Gallagher, chief executive of the Irish Hotels Federation, of a career in hospitality.

]]>Nick Bradshaw / The Irish Times<![CDATA[After the SuperValu cyberattack, your smart fridge might be the next target. Here’s what you need to know]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:41:50 +0000Do you feel differently about your smart fridge?

The high-tech home hub allows you to check what food you have in, suggest recipes, and manage the family calendar, should you be able to afford its not-insignificant price tag.

But this week’s cyberattack on Supervalu’s refrigeration systems might be forcing people to re-evaluate its position in their home.

Where could the next attack come from?

You might equally be eyeing your connected coffeemaker warily, worried about what it could be getting up to behind your back. You might consider unplugging the robot vacuum cleaner in case it goes rogue while you are out on the school run.

Jokes aside, the recent spate of attacks on seemingly harmless systems should give us pause for thought. The problem with many of these connected devices is that as soon as you hook anything up to the internet, it opens up a chink in your armour , no matter how hard we try to lock it down.

It is a trade-off that we might not be aware we are making at the time – but it is a common thread in the modern world. For the sake of convenience, we give up a little security. Even with the most diligent company in charge of maintaining the security of the appliances, there is always a risk that something will go wrong. And with the growth in artificial intelligence (AI), the chance of a previously undetected vulnerability rearing its head has suddenly been magnified.

You might wonder why hackers would want to attack a smart home device in the suburbs of Dublin. While we may not have thousands of euro of stock to destroy, or disposable income to pay out ransoms, we do have something that is valuable: our data. And that, as we know, is worth a lot of money in the right – or wrong – hands.

There is also the chance that our smart home devices, unpatched and open to exploitation, may be used as part of an attack on a high-value target.

Stop the bots: Six key steps to securing your smart home

In recent days, a joint operation between public and private partners in the tech industry took down a global botnet that had been hidden in set-top boxes across 200 countries. The botnet, which was placed on the devices before they were sold, surreptitiously used the set-top boxes and internet connections of those unlucky enough to have installed them in their homes.

This is not a new threat. Botnets have been carrying out large-scale attacks for years. One example: in 2016, the Mirai botnet took over up to 560,000 unsecured or weak cameras, printers, and DVR players and knocked out Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix, among others.

So what can we do to protect ourselves? Besides cutting off the connection, that is, although you could argue there is no compelling need to have an oven or coffee maker with an internet connection.

There is some help on the way from the bureaucrats, with various rules regarding security being implemented at an EU level, forcing manufacturers to adopt a secure-by-design approach. But we can’t rely on them to fully shield us from all the risks.

There are ways to protect ourselves: keeping up to date with software releases to patch up any security holes is a given;buying reputable brands rather than settling for cheap, unbranded technology from online marketplaces is another. Changing the default passwords on devices is another tip from security experts.

But we need to be aware of what could be coming down the line.

Anthropic recently warned of another threat: that AI models are becoming so smart and small in terms of storage requirements that they could copy themselves into places you might not suspect – such as your smart fridge.

That could create an army of smart botnets that could, in theory, be commanded to launch attacks without needing a data centre to run from. And, the experts argue, that would be one that is very difficult to battle, because there is no centralised point from where the attack has been launched.

Of course it is never as simple as it looks. The scenario proposed by Anthropic was a test rather than a real-world incident, and the end result – a model that replicates itself – is more of a ‘could’ than a ‘did’. The model didn’t have to break in as such, although we are often so lax about security on these connected devices that it wouldn’t have presented a huge barrier if that had been the case.

There are a few lessons to learn here.

Take the claims of AI companies about the power and potential of their technology with a grain of salt, for both good and bad.

But perhaps, to be safe, you might also consider limiting smart technology to the essentials. Sometimes the trade-off just isn’t worth it.

“It is rare that we see a targeted attack. What is often happening is that companies are victims of a bigger attack that is aimed at a weakness in software,” Honan says.

The speed of the attacks are also picking up pace, as are the scale of them. That was brought home this week with the cyberattack that hit grocery retailers across Europe, including in Ireland.

For the staff of Supervalu, it may have taken a while to grasp the full extent of the problem. Early morning alarm call-outs in retail are nothing too unusual; in some cases, they are false alarms that need nothing more than a cursory check.

But in the early hours of Monday morning, it became quickly apparent that the problem was a serious one. Across 13 Supervalu stores, refrigeration units showed abnormal temperature readings. The monitoring system in place to pick up on such issues had worked effectively, alerting managers to the emerging situation and allowing them to take swift action.

The problem could have been much worse. A spokesman for the company said it was a particular type of refrigeration unit that was impacted, which meant the majority of the 228 stores in the Supervalu network escaped. But for those who were severely affected – Lucan, Blanchardstown, Bray, Waterford – the cost of the incident could run into thousands of euro. Unable to guarantee that food had been stored at correct temperatures, the retailer had to dump stock, leading to rows of empty shelves.

SuperValu cyberattack reminds us that nobody is immune

It would take days for things to return to normal, with the precarious nature of food supply chains exposed in the process. Supermarkets work to keep food waste to a minimum by operating a “just-in-time” model for some stock that sees orders placed only when needed rather than keeping large back stocks of items just in case.

But with an incident of this nature, that meant some stock would take time to replenish.

The incident should serve as a warning shot, not just to the food retail business but to the wider business community.

Badly disrupted

Last year, Marks and Spencer found its business badly disrupted by a major cyber incident that left it unable to sell some of its products online for weeks. Jaguar Land Rover was also hit by a major attack, considered one of the most economically damaging in British history with an estimated cost of £1.9 billion (€2.3 billion) to the economy.

The company was forced to shut down automated production lines across its factories for five weeks, costing it £196 million directly and impacting thousands of businesses across the supply chain.

Closer to home, Jones Engineering was hit by a major ransomware attack in 2021, with hackers demanding millions for the return of its data. The company did not pay the ransom, instead bringing in outside security experts to restore its systems. That was closely followed by the attack on the HSE that took down computer systems in the health system, disrupted appointments and services, and saw the health data of thousands of people exposed.

There is a common thread with the attacks: social engineering and compromised credentials feature strongly. Workers are increasingly on their guard to avoid falling victim.

But even the most diligent of people can be caught out. John* found his email account taken hostage when he opened a link that came from a colleague. What he didn’t know was that the colleague had also fallen victim to a scam and had their email account taken over. “The first thing I did was check the address was genuine,” he says. “I wondered why they were sending me an email that AI had clearly been used to write. But I was skimming it and clicked the link. As soon as I did it, I realised what had happened.”

He immediately alerted the in-house IT staff, who had everything locked down within 20 minutes. But in that short space of time, hackers had managed to get into his email account and send the same message to all his contacts in an effort to dupe them. What he didn’t realise until the following day was that they had also implemented rules on his email account to bypass his inbox, feeding all the email into another folder.

Hundreds of messages were sent out in the 20-minute window. The hackers even replied to some who had messaged back to ask if the message was genuine.

“It was the first time any of us got caught out because it looks like it was from a colleague,” he says. “We did all the normal checks you would do, and when we realised what had happened we were straight on it.”

It is a common tactic that industry watchers are noting.

“Identity is becoming the new perimeter. Previously, a lot of the focus was on trying to secure your network, but increasingly attackers are targeting individuals to gain access to their digital identities, credentials, privileged accounts, and ultimately end up logging in rather than breaking in to your platforms,” says Stephen O’Keeffe of PwC. “Ransomware remains a big concern, and while originally it was about encrypting systems and causing disruption, increasingly there is a data theft component to it now.”

So where do businesses turn for help? Ireland has a cluster of big-name cybersecurity companies with their European bases here, such as Trend Micro, Fortinet, Malwarebytes and SolarWinds. But there is also an expanding home-grown sector, providing a launch pad for new enterprises, with companies such as Tines, Siren, UrbanFox and Cytidel going global from Ireland. According to Enterprise Ireland, there are 140 “pure play” cybersecurity companies located here, both Irish and foreign-owned.

In 2024, there were more than 8,100 cybersecurity professionals employed in Ireland. It is an area that seems destined to grow, even as AI takes over some of the load.

AI is also playing an outsized role in stoking fears. When the PHP vulnerability was discovered recently, it was down to AI. The flaw in the scripting language, which is used by a significant number of websites on the internet, had been present for a decade, escaping detection by human reviewers. But AI unearthed it, prompting immediate action from website owners who had to patch systems urgently.

AI-fuelled wave

There are fears of an AI-fuelled wave of sophisticated attacks, and it is colouring views of the technology as a whole. A survey conducted in September by technology consultants Expleo found that more than half of Irish business leaders are concerned about the cybersecurity risks posed by the technology, while 29 per cent said their opinion has been negatively impacted by their inability to successfully address cybersecurity and data protection risks.

That view has been driven in no small part by the AI companies themselves. In August, an open letter signed by some of the major players in AI – OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic – and cybersecurity and financial firms warned that an AI-driven wave of cyberattacks was on the way. Organisations have a narrow window to defend themselves, the letter warned.

We might not be there yet, but AI is playing a role. “I can honestly say I have never seen an attack where AI is the key element behind it,” Honan says. “But we are seeing attackers become more efficient and effective by using AI.”

Could the Australian health service website hack happen in Ireland?

That includes using AI to craft more convincing phishing emails, or reverse engineering software patches to launch attacks on systems that may have yet to shore up their defences. The window to patch these flaws is getting smaller, and companies need to prepare for more frequent software updates as both sides of the business use AI to stay a step ahead.

EY’s Puneet Kukreja compares leaving unpatched devices on a company network to a broken window in your home. “They don’t need to get to your core financial crown jewel assets to bring you down. They can simply go in and attack the lowest hanging fruit,” he says.

The problem though is identifying the low-hanging fruit. In some cases, the affected systems are not in the control of the companies that suffer the consequences but are a third-party service provider.

This is where a resilience and recovery plan can help mitigate some of the worst effects, to help identify the risks and also to minimise the damage.

“Organisations increasingly recognise that they cannot prevent every incident. So their attention is shifting toward detection, containing and business continuity,” PwC’s O’Keefe says. “It isn’t a matter of preventing every attack. It is how well you operate through and recover from one.”

*Names have been changed

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447417/">
   <title>‚Eiserne Lady‘ kehrt als ‚Action-Oma‘ zurück</title>
   <description>„Eiserne Lady“ Südafrikas wurde sie einst wegen ihrer Durchsetzungskraft genannt – nun ist der 75-jährigen Helen Zille mit einem teils skurrilem Wahlkampf als „Action-Oma“ ein Comeback gelungen. Wie am Samstag bekanntwurde, holte sie mit ihrer liberalen Demokratischen Allianz (DA) eine deutliche Mehrheit bei den Kommunalwahlen in Johannesburg, einer Stadt, die angesichts riesiger Probleme als unregierbar gilt. Seit 2019 gaben sich hier einander schon zehn Bürgermeister die Klinke in die Hand.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447559/">
   <title>Schussangriff laut Tusk „Terrorismus“</title>
   <description>Nach dem tödlichen Schussangriff im Zentrum der polnischen Stadt Krakau hat Polens Premier Donald Tusk von einem Akt des „Terrorismus“ gesprochen. Ein Mann hatte Samstagnachmittag sechs Menschen erschossen. 16 weitere wurden verletzt, darunter laut Innenministerium eine Person aus Österreich. Zuvor dürfte der Verdächtige zudem nahe Angehörige getötet haben. Laut Polens Innenminister war der mutmaßliche Schütze von „rechtsextremen Ideologien fasziniert“.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447410/">
   <title>Demokrat vor Sensation in Mississippi</title>
   <description>Den Erdrutschsieg bei den US-Midterms haben die Demokraten vor allem ihren Erfolgen in vielen republikanischen Hochburgen zu verdanken, etwa Texas und Kansas. Ob ihre Mehrheit im Senat noch eindeutiger ausfällt, steht noch aus. Allerdings bahnt sich im erzkonservativen Bundesstaat Mississippi eine Sensation an: Der Demokrat Scott Colom könnte dort der erste demokratische Senator in über 40 Jahren sowie der erste schwarze Senator in dem Südstaat seit den 1880er Jahren werden. Geschafft hat er das auch mit einem auffälligen Wahlkampf.</description>

   <title>Kritik an E-Card-Gebühr für Pensionisten</title>
   <description>Versicherten der Österreichischen Gesundheitskasse (ÖGK) wird einmal pro Jahr eine Servicegebühr für die E-Card verrechnet, für 2027 sind es knapp 27 Euro. Nach einem Regierungsbeschluss im Vorjahr müssen erstmals auch Pensionistinnen und Pensionisten bezahlen, die Gebühr wird ab November automatisch von der Pension abgezogen.    <title>Hängepartie nach Wahl in Neuseeland</title>
   <description>Neuseeland steht wohl vor einer schwierigen Regierungsbildung: Bei der Parlamentswahl am Samstag (Ortszeit) haben sich die konservative National Party von Ministerpräsident Christopher Luxon und die sozialdemokratische Labour-Partei des Herausforderers Chris Hipkins ein Kopf-an-Kopf-Rennen geliefert. Nach Auszählung von mehr als 95 Prozent der Stimmen lagen die beiden großen Parteien des Landes mit jeweils rund 29 Prozent der Stimmen nahezu gleichauf. Kleinere Parteien dürften somit eine entscheidende Rolle spielen.</description>

Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Sat, 07 Nov 2026 23:56:12 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 Six killed in terrorist shooting in Polish city of Kraków https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/07/fatalities-reported-in-shooting-on-historical-market-square-in-krakow/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:40:50 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106484
