    Chery’s new electric SUV is comfortable, roomy and loaded with kit, and it’s a close relative of the Jaecoo 7 that topped Britain’s sales chart in September. I drove a pre-production car in China, and if you want an EV with a name people will ask about in the company car park, it deserves a look, though the price will decide whether it deserves your money.

    Lepas L6 EV price and UK launch date

    The Lepas L6 EV is a comfortable, roomy electric family SUV with a long kit list and an official range of up to 279 miles, and on my drive it earned a place on any electric SUV shortlist. The steering is its weak spot, and the value case can’t be judged until Lepas names a price.

    That price hasn’t been announced yet, but order books are due to open in the final quarter of this year, and dealers are already taking registrations of interest. The brand is on sale here already with the L8, a bigger plug-in hybrid SUV that costs £34,900 in Essence trim and £37,900 as an Elevate, which shows where Lepas is pitching itself. Motorpoint expects the L6 to start at around £30,000 to £32,000.

    I drove a pre-production L6 EV over several days between Shanghai and Chery’s headquarters in Wuhu. It impressed me with its comfort and straightforward performance, although the steering felt artificial.

    The L6 shares its technology with the Jaecoo 7, Chery’s plug-in hybrid SUV that was the UK’s best-selling car in September, and it joins Chery, Omoda, Jaecoo and the L8 in the company’s push into Britain. Its electric rivals include the Skoda Elroq, Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.4.

    Who makes Lepas, and why does it exist?

    Lepas is Chery’s newest brand, launched in April 2025. At the 2026 Chery International User Summit in Wuhu, which was the other reason I was in China, I asked Zhong Wei, Lepas’s deputy chief executive, why the world needed it.

    For Mr Zhong, the brand reflects a shift in what buyers want. As people become more discerning, he says, they look for a car that expresses their personality and taste as well as getting them from A to B. Chery’s existing brands can’t satisfy every customer in the same way, he explained, so the company created a marque with its own identity, built around what he calls an elegant lifestyle of new-energy vehicles, intelligent technology and a more considered ownership experience.

    That’s a big ask in Britain, where plenty of company-car drivers and private buyers have stuck with European badges for years. They’ll want to know what a Lepas is worth after three years, and because the brand is so new here, there’s no track record to tell them.

    What is the Lepas L6 EV like to drive?

    I drove the L6 EV on multi-lane expressways, across the flat roads of the Yangtze River Delta and along more scenic mountain routes.

    It felt comfortable throughout, and acceleration was strong enough to make overtaking straightforward without the abrupt surge some electric cars produce. It also stayed composed on faster roads, in rain or shine (the part of China we were in seemed to deliver four seasons in one day). The cabin had enough room for four of us and our luggage, so it made a relaxed family car.

    The L6’s main weakness is its steering, which lacks the feedback you get from some European brands. If all you want is a comfortable, easy SUV, you’ll barely notice, but if you enjoy a more connected drive, it’s the part of the L6 most likely to disappoint.

    These impressions are based on a pre-production car, so the finished UK version may have different suspension and steering settings.

    Lepas L6 EV range and charging

    The L6 pairs a 65kWh battery with an electric motor producing 217PS and 275Nm of torque. Lepas quotes a 0 to 62mph time of 7.9 seconds and an official WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

    Driving in China isn’t always easy, especially in downpours (it’s almost as tricky as London), so I kept my eyes on the road rather than the instruments for much of the trip. We covered 360km (223 miles) in a day on fairly fast expressways, in humid weather with the air-con running the whole time, and the range never became a worry.

    Efficiency on that route hovered around 3.5 miles per kWh. That works out at roughly 225 miles from a full battery, about 50 miles short of the official figure, which is a fair result for fast driving in the heat with the air-con on, and it should cover most commutes for several days between charges.

    Maximum DC charging power is 120kW, and Lepas says a 30 to 80 per cent top-up takes about 22 minutes. How the L6 copes with a British winter and UK chargers is something I’ll find out on the UK-spec drive.

    Lepas L6 EV interior, boot space and technology

    The dashboard has a 13.2-inch touchscreen and an 8.88-inch digital driver’s display, and the system is quick and easy to use. There’s also a Hello Lepas voice assistant, which I didn’t try because I don’t speak Chinese. The cameras are crystal clear, making parking a doddle even when you’re jetlagged in the middle of a Chinese service station, and I think they’d earn their keep in tight city streets and underground car parks, especially in London.

    There are only two trims, Essence and Elevate. Both get 19-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic sunroof, a heated steering wheel and windscreen, 50W wireless phone charging, a 540-degree camera system, 22 driver-assistance functions and a 3.3kW vehicle-to-load socket. The Elevate adds heated and ventilated, electrically adjustable front seats, leather-effect upholstery, a power tailgate, an eight-speaker Sony stereo and parking assistance that includes remote parking. My pre-production car seemed to mix equipment from both, with fabric seats in place of the Elevate’s leather-effect finish.

    We drove four-up for most of the trip, and there’s room for three across the back seat. All our luggage went into the 410-litre boot, which grows to 1,334 litres with the rear seats folded (we didn’t need to try that), and a 99-litre compartment under the floor is handy for charging cables or a work laptop you’d rather keep out of sight.

    Lepas L6 EV company car tax and running costs

    For company-car drivers, the L6 sits on the same 4 per cent benefit-in-kind rate as any electric car in the 2026/27 tax year, rising to 5 per cent from April 2027. If it were priced at £35,000, in line with the L8, that would be roughly £560 a year in tax for a 40 per cent taxpayer and £280 for a basic-rate one.

    Private buyers will want to see the price before judging value, but the warranty is reassuring, with seven years or 100,000 miles on the car and eight years or 100,000 miles on the battery. RAC roadside cover comes free for the first year and can be renewed for up to seven years if you service the car at a Lepas dealer.

    Is the Lepas L6 EV worth buying?

    The L6 EV has the makings of a credible electric family SUV, with useful performance, a practical cabin and a long list of standard kit. The big unanswered question is value.

    What we like

    • A claimed range of up to 279 miles, and about 225 miles in hot, fast real-world driving.
    • Comfortable cruising and plenty of room for a family and its luggage.
    • A long list of standard technology, including a 540-degree camera system that makes parking easy.

    What worries us

    • Steering that felt artificial.
    • No confirmed UK price.
    • Unknown resale values for a brand that’s new to Britain.

    If the L6 is on your list for when orders open, find out what your current car is worth with Regit’s free valuation, so you know how much a part-exchange could knock off the price.

    Verdict

    The Lepas L6 EV deserves a place on your electric SUV shortlist, because it’s comfortable and spacious, has a boot you wouldn’t turn your nose up at, and comes with a camera system that takes the stress out of tight streets and underground car parks. The steering needs work, though, and the L6 still has to prove itself on British roads.

    Until Lepas confirms UK pricing, the value case is a blank, and with the L8 already at £34,900 the L6 needs to come in well below that. Get the number right and it could be a serious alternative to better-known electric SUVs such as the Skoda Elroq. I’ll be driving a UK-spec car in the coming weeks, and I’ll update this review when I have.

    Whoever bought a BMW i7 new three years ago has watched well over half its price disappear, which is rotten luck for them and a gift for anyone shopping second-hand. Better still, a luxury EV registered before April 2025 escapes a tax that a new one pays for five years.

    If you’ve ever fancied a BMW i7, the used market has made it a lot more realistic. Three-year-old cars are listed at dealers from about £45,000, according to AutoUncle listings we checked on 5 November, while the cheapest new i7 costs £104,230. Figures Auto Express published on 29 October show it’s part of a pattern, because the i7, Porsche Taycan, BMW i5, Audi e-tron GT and Mercedes EQS and EQE are all expected to be worth less than a third of their price new after three years and 36,000 miles.

    Those Auto Express numbers are forecasts of what a car bought new today will fetch in part-exchange, set against its average list price, or the price of one version where it names one. Dealers ask more than part-exchange value, and plenty of these cars were sold with hefty discounts, so not every first owner has lost quite this much, but the size of the drop shows you where the bargains are.

    Which luxury EVs lose the most value

    1. Porsche Taycan

    Average price new £162,255, expected value after three years about £50,475, so it’s expected to lose about £111,780.

    No electric car in Auto Express’s figures loses more cash, though the average is dragged up by Turbo S and Turbo GT versions costing well over £150,000, and 2023 cars are listed from about £51,000. A 2023 car is the version before the 2024 update, which Porsche says brought up to 35% more range, so look up the official range for the exact car you’re looking at rather than going by a new one’s brochure.

    2. BMW i7

    Average price new £143,530, expected value after three years about £46,050, so it’s expected to lose about £97,480.

    AutoUncle showed 21 three-year-old i7s for sale on 5 November, from £43,998, with most between about £47,000 and £63,000. Auto Express reckons the i7 is the wiser used buy of the two big electric limousines, ahead of the Mercedes EQS. Our motoring reporter Tim Barnes-Clay reviewed the facelifted 2026 i7, and two of the changes he found matter if you’re buying an older one. The update lifted BMW’s range figure to as much as 452 miles from 388, so a 2023 car won’t go as far on a charge, but it also took away the iDrive rotary controller, which Tim missed and which a 2023 car still has.

    3. BMW i5

    Average price new £110,045, expected value after three years about £34,650, so it’s expected to lose about £75,395.

    The i5 is the electric 5 Series, long the default choice in the executive car park. Auto Express’s average is higher than the list price of even the top i5 M60 Touring (£98,425), so treat the cash figure as rough, but keeping about 31% of its value is the number that matters. It only went on sale in late 2023, so used ones are mostly 2024 cars or newer, and that’s fine for tax, because what counts is the date the car was first registered.

    4. Audi e-tron GT

    Price new £107,875 for the S e-tron GT, expected value after three years about £33,150, so it’s expected to lose about £74,725.

    The e-tron GT shares its underpinnings with the Taycan, so it’s the closest thing to a Porsche with four rings on the bonnet. Auto Express’s figures are for today’s S e-tron GT, while 2023 cars are the earlier e-tron GT quattro, and used ones are thinner on the ground. One we found, a December 2023 car with about 13,700 miles, was up for £46,850, which AutoUncle reckons is about £5,000 more than it’s worth.

    5. Mercedes EQS

    Price new £104,540 for the EQS 450+ Premium, expected value after three years about £32,375, so it’s expected to lose about £72,165.

    The EQS gives you S-Class space and quiet without an engine, and 2023 EQS 450+ saloons were listed from about £41,500 on 5 November. Auto Express isn’t a fan, though, and says rivals including the i7 are simply better all-round packages.

    6. Mercedes EQE

    Price new £86,615 for the EQE 350+ AMG Line Night Edition, expected value after three years about £26,850, so it’s expected to lose about £59,765.

    The EQE is the smaller EQS, roughly an electric E-Class, and it’s the cheapest way into this club. AutoUncle had 29 three-year-old EQE 300s for sale on 5 November, between about £29,000 and £37,000, which is about what a new Volkswagen Golf costs. Cheaper electric cars lose even more in percentage terms, led by the Lexus UX 300e, and we’ve rounded those up separately.

    Why a used luxury EV is cheaper to tax

    What matters is the date on the log book. GOV.UK’s vehicle tax rate tables say any electric car first registered before 1 April 2025 never pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement, however much it cost new, so it pays the £200 standard rate. Electric cars registered since then pay £10 in their first year, then £640 a year for the next five if their list price was over £50,000, which covers every car on this list.

    That’s £2,200 over five years that a car registered before April 2025 never pays. October’s Budget raises the standard rate to £210 from April 2027, but the gap stays, and our guide to this year’s car tax changes covers the rest of the rates. Check the first registration date on the V5C before you buy, because an i5 registered in March 2025 and one registered in April look the same on the forecourt but don’t cost the same to tax.

    In London, any electric car is ULEZ-free, and the Congestion Charge is £13.50 a day rather than £18 as long as the car is registered for Auto Pay, while plug-in hybrids pay the full £18. That matters if you want a 7 Series, because in 2023 BMW UK sold it only as the electric i7 or as a plug-in hybrid such as the 750e. Drive a 2023 750e into the zone on about 230 working days a year and the charge comes to £4,140, against £3,105 in an i7, so the i7 saves £1,035. Add the £440 supplement the 750e pays until its sixth year on the road and the i7 comes out almost £1,500 a year ahead. From April 2028, though, electric cars will also pay 3p a mile on top of road tax, which is about £270 a year if you cover 9,000 miles, and Regit has worked out what pay-per-mile tax will cost you at other mileages.

    What to check before you buy

    A 2023 car will only just have had its first MOT, so the service history tells you more than the MOT record. Ask for a battery health report, which shows how much of the original capacity is left, and check how long the battery warranty has to run. Make sure both charging cables come with the car, look at the tyres (heavy EVs get through them quickly) and get an insurance quote before you fall for one, because a car that’s cheap to buy is still expensive to insure.

    When you’ve found the one, put its number plate into Regit’s free car valuation and you’ll know whether the dealer’s price for that i7 or EQS is fair before you start haggling.

    Our verdict

    Let someone else pay for the first three years. A 2023 BMW i7 from about £45,000 is our pick, because it has a back seat built for being driven around in, keeps the rotary controller the new one has lost and costs £200 a year to tax. If you’d rather drive than be driven, the Taycan from about £51,000 is the more exciting car, and the EQE from £29,000 is the cheapest way in, but whichever you choose, get the battery checked and the insurance quoted before you sign.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

A couch-surfing guest from Munich learned about the site, liked it, and helped carry the idea into Germany, where it launched under its own local name, Kleiderkreisel. In 2025 it also opened operations in Latvia, Estonia and Slovenia, seventeen years after that first Vilnius website, extending its reach into corners of Europe the original Kleiderkreisel-era patchwork of local sites never touched.

From a free site to a billion-dollar company

The money that built out Vinted’s logistics network came in stages, and the pace of it tracks how quickly investors decided the model was working. In November 2019, the company raised €128 million in a round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with Accel, Insight Partners, Sprints Capital and Burda Principal Investments also participating, pushing its valuation past $1 billion for the first time and making it, according to the reporting on the round, Lithuania’s first unicorn. Lightspeed partner Brad Twohig said at the time the firm looked for “outlier management teams building generational companies,” a fairly standard line for a venture press release, but one that in this case was describing two people who had started out solving a problem for their own friends.

Two years later, in 2021, a further round led by EQT Growth brought in $303 million and roughly quadrupled the valuation again, to $4.5 billion, with the same core group of earlier investors returning. That was the last outside funding round before the company turned its first profit in 2023, at which point continued growth could increasingly be funded from the business itself rather than from new investors.

What the 2025 numbers actually show

Vinted’s first profitable year, by its own account, was 2023, when it reported revenue of €596.3 million and a net profit of €17.8 million, a milestone The Next Web covered as the company’s first since founding. Two years later, the picture is bigger but less straightforwardly better. Vinted moved €10.8 billion in gross merchandise value in 2025, up 47 percent on the year before, and took €1.1 billion of that as revenue, up 38 percent, almost double the 2023 figure. But net profit, which had grown substantially in the years after 2023, fell 19 percent in 2025 to €62 million, and adjusted EBITDA slipped 5 percent to €151 million. CEO Thomas Plantenga framed the trade-off plainly in the release: the company is spending on expansion, including a push into Germany, category diversification beyond clothing, and the launch of a payments wallet called Vinted Pay, rather than banking the growth as profit this year.

That is a company reinvesting in expansion while remaining profitable, not a company in trouble. It is worth naming the distinction because the two can look similar on a spreadsheet, and a 19 percent drop in profit reads very differently once it’s clear the company was profitable at all only two years earlier, and is still profitable now, just less so by design.

A platform built on other people’s closets

What the €10.8 billion figure represents is how far secondhand clothing has moved from a hobby into ordinary consumer behaviour across Europe. The company has said it intends to bring the same model to the United States next, according to Dealroom’s coverage of the 2025 results. Whether Vinted’s European logistics playbook, built over seventeen years and hundreds of thousands of parcel points, transfers to a market with a completely different postal and returns infrastructure is the open question the 2025 numbers don’t answer.

Rapidly changing feed content may increase task switching and decision-making, which can make scrolling feel mentally tiring.]]>

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

]]> In a series of staged online sales, people selling a used gadget with a known flaw often owned up to it more than buyers predicted — the sellers reported caring more about honesty and fairness, and less about the price, than the buyers assumed https://siliconcanals.com/s-in-a-series-of-staged-online-sales-people-selling-a-used-gadget-with-a-known-flaw-often-owned-up-to-it-more-than-buyers-predicted-the-sellers-reported-caring-more-about-honesty-and-fairness-and/ Fri, 18 Sep 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109366

Across five studies of secondhand-market haggling, sellers were often more candid than buyers expected. Three minutes of small talk before the haggling narrowed the gap, and so did asking buyers to think about the seller's conscience first.]]>

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

They’re often people whose sense of dignity was undermined so regularly that protecting it became something close to a full-time occupation https://siliconcanals.com/d-psychology-suggests-people-who-appear-offended-by-everything-arent-usually-seeking-drama-theyre-often-people-whose-sense-of-dignity-was-undermined-so-regularly-that-protecting-it-became-something-c/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:02 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109377

Chronic offense-taking isn't performative outrage—it's a trauma response masquerading as oversensitivity.]]>

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

The post Robot integration brings high-precision production to midmarket manufacturers appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

High-precision manufacturing was once considered something exclusive to large corporations. However, advances in robotic integration and automated manufacturing have changed this perception.

Sophisticated capabilities are becoming accessible to midmarket and smaller operations. This shift has led to a more even competitive landscape.

Smaller manufacturers have an opportunity to reach new levels of accuracy and efficiency. Today’s robotic systems can help these producers modernize targeted workflows without overhauling their entire production operations.

Robotic innovations drive efficiency for manufacturers

The evolution of robotics has led to more democratized precision manufacturing processes. This is evident across industrial robots and agile collaborative robots.

Key benefits of these innovations can include:

  • Cost and footprint: The potential for lower investment costs and compact designs can make robotic systems economically viable. It can also simplify integration into existing layouts.
  • Enhanced programming: Intuitive interfaces and lead-through teaching methods support quick deployment and reconfiguration. This reduces the training typically required for operators without robotics expertise.
  • Sensors and AI-driven capabilities: Sensors, such as vision systems and force-torque sensors, can be integrated with AI. This enables robots to understand, react and adapt with precision.
  • Safety and collaboration: Cobots can work safely alongside humans without extensive guarding. This fosters a flexible human-robot workforce that combines optimal utilization and human dexterity.

These advancements mean that midmarket manufacturers can overcome hurdles like skilled labor shortages, rising costs, and quality demands.

Submit your innovation now!

Real-world impact of robotic integration for precision manufacturers

Here are some use cases that show how a diverse range of manufacturers have taken advantage of recent advances in robotics.

1. SCHUNK R-C2 automation for flexible production

Torneria Novoletto is an Italian organization specializing in sophisticated components for the chemical, medical, and pharmaceutical sectors.

The company faced obstacles in achieving high precision and process reliability for medium-sized batches. It implemented SCHUNK’s R-C2 automation concept, integrating advanced clamping devices and grippers with robotic handling.

Introducing this system helped to support high operational flexibility. Setup and changeover times were also significantly reduced because the SCHUNK R-C2 allows the continuous handling of workpiece sizes and automated reclamping.

This innovative robotic integration has helped Torneria Novoletto to pursue an unmanned 24/7 operation, increase machine utilization, and mitigate shortages of skilled labor.

Torneria Novoletto shows the compact efficiency of the R-C2 automation. Source: SCHUNK

2. Cobot integration for part marking

Telesis, a leading provider of industrial marking solutions, integrated its part marking technology with systems from Universal Robots.

The company offers advanced laser and dot peen markers. When a Telesis laser marking system is integrated with a UR force- and power-limited robot arm, it creates a precise and flexible method of identifying automated parts.

Innovations like this ensure that systems can be safely deployed alongside human workers. Robotic integrations have provided Telesis with a streamlined marking process without complex safety enclosures, consistent high-quality marking on various materials and part geometries, and added traceability and quality control.

Telesis demonstrates integrated laser-marking systems with robotic control. Source: Universal Robots

3. FANUC M-20 robots enhance throughput and scale

Northern Kentucky Machine (NKM), a flexible job shop, experienced labor shortages and production capacity challenges. Its strategic response included the use of automated manufacturing solutions, such as deploying FANUC M-20 Series industrial robots.

By using Automation Within Reach’s (AWR) “RC-2” CNC machine-tending system, the integration increased NKM’s throughput and machine utilization.

Operators quickly adapted to programming and running these robotic cells. This helped to enable “lights-out” manufacturing for longer runs, freeing up human workers for other tasks.

The FANUC robots have provided NKM with the scalability needed to pursue and take on larger projects, deliver consistent part quality, drive growth, and compete with other midsize organizations.

NKM used the M-20 Series robot to boost the efficiency of human workers. Source: FANUC

4. ActiNav enables bin picking and legacy equipment extension

PrecisionForm Inc. is a producer of small custom metal parts. It faced the challenge of automating bin picking for CNC machines.

By deploying Universal Robots’ ActiNav system, PrecisionForm integrated a UR5 cobot with advanced vision and path-planning capabilities. This approach led to reliable part picking from deep bins that were then loaded into CNC machines.

Challenging geometries were less of an issue, and operators were freed up to manage multiple machines. The UR cobots helped reduce labor challenges and extend the lifespan of older CNC equipment.

By adding a relatively inexpensive robotic solution, PrecisionForm Inc gained additional utility from existing machinery, increased the potential return on investment (ROI) as a midmarket operation, and improved daily production.

Uses can easily deploy and calibrate the ActiNav system, says UR. Source: Universal Robots

Capabilities evolve for midmarket manufacturers

The accessibility of precision manufacturing marks a crucial moment for many industries. Robotic integration is no longer exclusive to the world’s largest enterprises.

Innovations offering ultra-high accuracy and consistent quality are now economically and operationally viable for midsized manufacturers. The benefits that organizations such as Telesis, Torneria Novoletto, NKM, and PrecisionForm now have shown that modern robotics can drive sustainable growth.

Robotic solutions continue to evolve. As they do, the advantages of automated manufacturing will grow alongside those changes. With thoughtful and careful implementation, a new generation of agile and highly precise manufacturers will be waiting to reap the benefits of this exciting new world.

About the author

Lou Farrell, a senior editor at Revolutionized, has written on the topics of robotics, computing, and technology for years. He has a great passion for the stories he covers and for writing in general.

The post Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

The new Stretch features an updated modular design that enables “plug and play” part swaps. | Source: Boston Dynamics

Boston Dynamics Inc. this week unveiled Stretch Gen 2, the latest generation of its autonomous mobile trailer unloading robot. With over 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes handled under its belt, the company built the updated robot to maximize uptime and streamline maintenance.

Brian Donnelly, the vice president and general manager of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, told The Robot Report that the company has been working on the new version of Stretch for around two and a half years.

“When we made the first generation of Stretch, we were focused on trying to get a product out into the market as fast as possible and really get it in customers’ hands and get it operational,” he said. “It was not the easiest to manufacture; there were a lot of components.”

“[With Stretch 2], we really were focused on simplification, hardening the robot, and really driving improved reliability and performance,” added Donnelly. “That’s really what drove a lot of our decisions was just making the robot better in every way.”

Stretch Gen 2 can unload up to 1,000 cases per hour. This rate is highly dependent on factors such as case weight and how neat or disorderly cases are stacked. It has a multipick feature, a battery that can last two shifts, and a fast charger that can get it to 90% charge in about 75 minutes.

The mobile manipulator also features onboard lighting, making it easier to work in dark trailers, and a pre-trained vision system that can detect most packages without programming needed.

Stretch’s hardware upgrades improve durability

Boston Dynamics geared many of Stretch Gen 2’s upgrades towards reducing downtime and making the robot more durable. For example, the Waltham, Mass.-based company also cut 81% of the internal cabling, around half a mile’s worth.

“[Cabling] is weight, it’s cost, and its points of failure, particularly when you have something that’s in constant motion, you’re creating strain on those cables with every motion,” Donnelly said. “If you don’t have good strain relief, you don’t have good ways of managing the cables in the robot. It can cause stress on the cables and then failure.”

Donnelly said Hyundai helped the company source a cable harness through its automotive supply chain. This isn’t the only thing Boston Dynamics learned from the automotive industry. Stretch Gen 2 uses heavy-duty automotive-grade connectors. These hold up to the vibration of rapid, high-torque box handling and driving over uneven floors.

“In the automotive industry, they have to deal with a lot of real-world challenges in their vehicles. There’s a lot of miles driven dealing with shock and vibration and things like this,” Donnelly said. “As a robot moves around the world, just like a car, if you don’t have latching connectors, then they can sort of wiggle apart. By leveraging those automotive connectors, we’re much more confident that the connectors are going to stay latched together and not pull apart in the field.”

The robot also has continuous rotation joints that move beyond 360° so they no longer hit hard stops. This can help prevent previously caused mechanical stress. Donnelly pointed out this also makes the robot more productive, as it can completely optimize its trajectory planning and move in any direction.

The emergency stop on the robot now sits lower and is recessed. Boston Dynamics made the exterior panels with new materials so a falling box is far less likely to trip an unintentional safety stoppage or break a panel.

How Stretch Gen 2 gets a grip on multiple boxes

The gripper is the part of the robot that often deals with the most stress. It’s making contact with all of the the things the robot needs to handle. Stretch Gen 2 features an upgraded gripper with new valve systems and more precise sensing improves grasping and placement to optimize fast-paced picks.

“[The new gripper] has a value in every suction cup, which enables us to pick multiple boxes with a single motion of the arm, which substantially increases our throughput,” Donnelly explained. “If we can pick multiple boxes, with a single motion of the arm, we get much higher throughput because the pick cycle of picking up a box from the floor of a container and place it to a conveyor is dominated by arm movement. So, if we can keep the arm moving and just do more every cycle, that is really effective and improves the rate at which we can unload a truck for our customers.”

The new gripper is also better at configuring boxes on the conveyor belt in ways that work best for Boston Dynamics’ customers, and use less power in picking up boxes.

“Every cup is individually sensed and actuated, so we know when we have good suction,” said Donnelly. “We only have the value open to pull suction when we have good contact on a box, so that enables us to reduce the amount of power we’re spending running on the vacuum pump, so we’re not pulling suction through cups that don’t have good contact. It also enables us to, when we pick up those multiple boxes, singulate them onto the conveyor.”

Stretch Gen 2 brings service time down to just hours

With Stretch Gen 2, Boston Dynamics didn’t just want to reduce the frequency of service calls; it also wanted to make those service calls faster when they do happen.

“We didn’t have as much experience from a serviceability perspective as a company when we made the first-generation robot,” Donnelly said. “We’ve since deployed these robots, serviced them in the field, and hired a lot of people who have a lot more experience than we originally did in service. Their input and guidance really helped us to make a robot that’s much more manufacturable and more serviceable.”

The robot doesn’t require dynamic cables and complex harnesses. Instead it uses standardized high-strength fasteners to cut down on tool changes and hands-on repair time. For example, the company can perform a full swerve drive swap in just one hour. Before, this process could take an entire day.

Stretch Gen 2 also features new onboard diagnostics and maintenance tools. These put more routine service in the hands of a customer’s own maintenance team, so robots stay on the dock with less reliance on outside support.

Updated robot continuously improves its performance

The new robot runs on a redesigned onboard computing platform that is constantly improving. Boston Dynamics said it will regularly release software updates to bring gains in case detection, motion planning, pick strategies, and world modeling across an entire fleet, with no hardware changes required.

Donnelly said that with the company’s most recent update, it saw a 24% increase in unload rate across its fleet of fielded robots.

“A lot of our activity on this program is really focused on the software. We’re constantly improving our computer vision capabilities to be able to better perceive boxes and conveyors and container walls, and then really pick boxes and place them to convey more and more productivity over time,” Donnelly said.

Right now, Donnelly said Boston Dynamics releases new software, on average, on a monthly basis.

Submit your innovation now!

How have customers reacted to Gen 2 so far?

Donnelly said Boston Dynamics already has Stretch Gen 2 running at multiple customer sites.

“Customers are really happy with it, and they’re continuing to rely on it to do its work every day,” said Donnelly. “We’re going into these existing sites and deploying these robots within two weeks. The folks who are taking over operating the robots are the folks who are otherwise doing repetitive heavy lifting of these boxes and containers.”

“We put a lot of effort into ensuring that the user experience, from an operator perspective, is really simple. It doesn’t require a ton of training,” he added. “A person can drive the robot into a container, step out of the safety work cell, and they press a big Play button, and then the robot does the rest.”

Many of the people working with Stretch used to spend their days unloading heavy boxes from trailers.

“Fundamentally, unloading trailers is one of the worst jobs in the warehouse,” Donnelly said. “It can be really hot in a container that’s been sitting in a yard in the summer. It can be super cold in the winter. Then the work itself is moving heavy boxes repeatedly from down low or up high. It puts a lot of strain and stress on people’s bodies.”
