ABB Robotics has integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into RobotStudio. Source: ABB Robotics

Yesterday, ABB Robotics confirmed to The Robot Report that China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has blocked SoftBank Group Corp.’s planned acquisition of ABB Robotics. Regulators had expressed concern that data for training artificial intelligence models could be transferred overseas.

ABB Robotics is already a significant manufacturer and provider of robotics in China. The Zurich-based company stated that it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.”

Other countries are moving to protect what they view as sovereign physical AI. For instance, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) recently banned new models of certain connected advanced devices, including legged robots and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Companies such as Intel and Husqvarna have already received conditional approvals.

In addition, the U.S. Department of Commerce last week determined that imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and related components pose a threat to the U.S. economy and national security. This could lead to tariffs.

Government investigations can directly affect major robotics and AI companies. European antitrust scrutiny of Amazon’s proposed acquisition of iRobot was one reason why that deal was terminated, with iRobot subsequently entering bankruptcy proceedings. The robotic vacuum pioneer has since been picked up by Shenzhen, China-based Picea Robotics Co.

ABB Robotics as focused on automation and AI

ABB Robotics claimed that it is the only company whose integrated portfolio includes industrial automation, software, force- and power-limited cobots, and AMRs. The company said its “autonomous versatile robotics” help businesses of all sizes in industries including automotive, electronics, and logistics.

ABB Robotics has installed more than 500,000 robots around the world and employs about 7,000 people. Its U.S. headquarters are in Auburn Hills, Mich. In October 2025, parent company ABB said it had agreed to sell its robotics division to Japan-based SoftBank Group Corp. for $5.3 billion.

“Considering the intensive competition in traditional robotics, established manufacturers like ABB will need to lead the charge in AI-driven robotics to protect their margins,” said Samantha Mou, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis. “However, achieving this will require significant investment. The substantial long-term R&D costs may be a key factor behind ABB’s decision to sell its robotics business.”

“Compared with the other Big 4 vendors [FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa], ABB was already quick in combining AI with its products, which is an area where it can have synergy with SoftBank,” Mou told The Robot Report. She said that companies in Europe, Asia, and the Americas are hoping that AI, which has already been used for ease of programming, monitoring, and predictive maintenance, can be generalized to more processes.

“AI gives ABB Robotics considerable potential,” said Robert Little, a business development advisor and former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc, on LinkedIn. “But turning that potential into commercially useful systems requires sustained investment. In my humble opinion, backing that investment within ABB becomes a harder decision when robotics has to compete for funding against higher-margin businesses. ABB also saw limited synergies between robotics and the rest of the company.”

“SoftBank made sense,” he added. “ABB brings robot manufacturing, application expertise and established customer relationships. SoftBank could bring additional investment and a clear focus on AI.”

Sovereign physical AI becomes a strategic concern

“Post Astra, robotics data has become more strategic,” posted Financial Times reporter Zijing Wu, in reference to the GPT-6 model that OpenAI released in September and that Chinese AI firms used to train their models.

“The NDRC [China’s National Development and Reform Commission] had been concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas, where it could be used to train AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, in which SoftBank is a major investor, sources say,” said Wu on X.

Countries have become increasingly aware of the competitive advantage promised by the convergence of automation and AI.

“What makes this particularly significant is that industrial robotics is increasingly being viewed not simply as manufacturing equipment, but as strategically important technology at the intersection of automation, data, and AI,” Ash Sharma, managing director of Interact Analysis, told The Robot Report.

“China is a critical market for ABB Robotics, so separating the Chinese operation from a global transaction of this scale would be extremely challenging,” he added. “More broadly, this highlights how robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capability are becoming important considerations in cross-border M&A as physical AI develops.”

Ahmed Humayun, head of go to market for defense manufacturing at Gecko Robotics, posted to LinkedIn: “This move reflects Chinese concerns about asset transfers to Japan during a time of heightened Chinese-Japanese tension, but [it] also shows concerns about robotics data generated in China being transferred abroad to train foundation models. The most recent example of China flexing its economic muscle and demonstrating that it has many levers to prevent intellectual property and assets from leaving its soil — even when developed by foreign companies.”

“I was worried this might happen,” said Little. “Over the years, I have seen ABB‘s strength in China grow. Where do we go from here?”

“My take: ABB has built a strong presence in China, but heavily subsidized Chinese robot makers are becoming stronger competitors at home and expanding into Europe,” he wrote. “That creates more pressure on pricing and margins that were not that great to begin with fall even further.”

“There may still be negotiations that find a way forward,” concluded Little. “For now, ABB is in a pickle.”

]]>

Agility says its Digit 5 humanoids can lift up to 50 lb. | Source: Agility Robotics

Earlier today, Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker “AGLT.” The company claimed that it is “the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public.”

Agility started the day trading at $11.26 per share, above the initial $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. It was a day of ups and downs, as it was for many tech stocks. It hit its lowest price at $8.40, and its highest at $12.15.

The company ended up closing the day trading slightly above (2%) where it had started, at $11.49. Other pure-play robotics providers did not fare so well.

Serve Robotics, another publicly traded robotics company that offers sidewalk delivery robots, ended down 12.45%. Surgical robotics leader Intuitive Surgical ended down 2.82%. Symbotic, which provides end-to-end warehouse automation, ended down 2.47%. In addition, PROCEPT BioRobotics Corp., which provides robotic aquablation therapy, ended down 6.42%.

While Unitree, another humanoid robotics provider, doesn’t trade on the Nasdaq, it is public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s STR Market. It’s one of the only other publicly traded humanoid robot providers.

Unitree first debuted on the market at 150.80 yuan ($22.55 U.S.), and saw some quick success, hitting a high of 1,100 yuan ($164.46) that day. Just a few weeks after debuting on the market, it was down almost 53% from its first-day high. The company is still working to climb back up to those numbers.

In addition, China has reportedly tightened its own requirements for initial public offerings for humanoid robot startups.

Technology and AI-related stocks struggle across markets

Note that the entire Nasdaq is down 5.52% today, which means Agility was beating this overall trend. Much of these losses were concentrated in AI-related stocks.

NVIDIA ended the day down 9.26% from its opening price. AMD ended down 17.26%, while Qualcomm dropped 9.49%. Microsoft was down 3.58%. Rockwell Automation was down 14.15%.

Other markets have had some of their worst days since April 2025. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 3.44%.

This week’s midterm elections have caused the markets to fluctuate. While they saw some sharp gains yesterday, many of those gains dissipated today. Today’s losses have a lot to do with investor uncertainty around future data center buildouts with a now Democratically controlled Senate and House.

What comes next for Agility Robotics

From left to right, Cassie and Digit through the years. | Source: Agility Robotics

The Robot Report will be watching Agility’s performance on the markets in the coming months. Already, the company alluded to adding more robots to its portfolio. The Robot Report also broke the news about Agility exploring wheel-based robots in September 2026.

Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, talked more about this plan in a recent video. In the video, she mentioned the possible addition of a smaller bipedal form factor to the company’s lineup.

In hospitals, hygiene is critical. But the cleaning process, which is time-intensive and difficult to scale, remains manual work. This often means the process is also inconsistent. Healthcare facilities are under pressure to care for more patients with fewer resources. These challenges are why the Silicon & Embedded division at GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics engineer a mobile robot to handle disinfection.

The project started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when disinfection became a critical use case for robots.

“Obviously, this was a big use case at that point of time, in terms of being able to sanitize hospitals and care facilities,” Kunaal Mahanti, physical AI lead at GlobalLogic, told The Robot Report. “So [Haystack] came up with this concept of being able to do disinfection better.”

“While there were disinfections which are happening manually, it wasn’t really good coverage,” he added. “We were really the engineering and collaboration partner there to see how we can take this concept and make it.”

The result is an autonomous mobile robot (AMR) that combines real-time perception, edge-based intelligence, and navigation to deliver hospital-grade UV disinfection with minimal human intervention. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company said it can operate safety alongside people, interpret its surroundings, and adapt to changes in its environment.

GlobalLogic aims to create a scalable platform

When designing its robot, Mahanti said GlobalLogic didn’t want to just quickly design a system for one use case or environment.

“We wanted to make it an expandable platform,” he explained. “The idea was that you can look at, for example, the track part of it, which is the thing that is carrying the robot, independent of what it is carrying, which is the UV. Architecturally, you keep them separated so that we can mount other things at a later date.”

“It went from a concept to what would be an architectural foundation, so that it’s not just that one product,” said Mahanti. “It actually becomes a class of solutions that we can build for the same industry segment.”

While GlobalLogic hasn’t done many other deployments in hospitals, Mahanti did say the company used some of the base components of the UV robot for other projects.

“When you look at the platform that moves, there are things that have come out from there in terms of the control of the motors,” he said. “Then we use ROS to do the programming and the sensor fusion part, that is reusable, and we’ve used that. So, if not necessarily the same device, but that architecture broadly.”

Navigating the challenges that come with hospitals

Healthcare facilities are crowded, chaotic, and involve many closed-off spaces, making them difficult for robots to work in.

“The known part was that, obviously, you have to interact with humans. The unknown part is that there are doors, there are things that need to be opened, and you can’t always just barge in,” Mahanti said.

This is different from more common use cases for mobile robots in warehousing or manufacturing, which typically involve open-spaces that are easy to navigate

“There are two modes that we ended up building for [the robots],” noted Mahanti. “Essentially, one was this autonomous mode, where it would navigate and find the right room. The other was a ‘follow me’ mode, in which case it would follow a caregiver or a nurse.”

This means the caregiver can open doors and ensure spaces are ready for the robot to enter. It also means a patient wouldn’t be blindsided by a robot entering their room, for example.

However, designing an AMR that can work in these complex spaces has created benefits in other parts of GlobalLogic’s business. With a much higher bar for safety, the company could apply the platform to other industries.

“The other learning is just being able to be in an environment where you cannot be loud, for example, when we are designing the motors or looking at what we need to put in [the robot],” said Mahanti. “Those things are specific to this industry, but then dealing with that has helped us build machines with higher fidelity elsewhere, where it is not necessarily a given, but it’s a good thing to have. What’s holding back robotic adoption in hospitals?

While more robots are making their way into hospitals, most people cannot yet walk into their local hospitals and find robots roaming the halls. This is still an emerging area for robotics, so what challenges still exist? Mahanti said three things come to mind.

The first is cost. “There needs to be an ROI,” he replied. “For example, if you look at this use case during COVID, at that point of time, you needed less people in the hospitals. You needed to be safe. It was a big issue. So that ROI was justifiable.”

Second is compliance with medical standards, which becomes much trickier when deploying robots that will interact with the public and patients.

Third is the perception of robots. Mahanti acknowledged that hospital staffers don’t want a big, bulky robot taking up space in busy corridors and elevators.

“There are clearly safety concerns, from multiple angles. Navigating in a very human-crowded situation is not easy,” he said. “For a disinfectant use case, if a robot waits for people to keep moving and then slowly moves, you’re okay. For example, a robot might be able to navigate an emergency room in a perfect condition with no obstacles, but the addition of patients who constantly moving or being moved and staffers running around to solve critical issues make navigation much more challenging.

“The entire workflow within a hospital is built for humans. You can’t just fit a robot in thinking it’s a human. So, there is work to be done in converting some of the workflow, the spaces, everything,” Balasubramanian said.

LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a world action model (WAM) pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. The Beijing-based startup said the model combines human video with glove-recorded motion and embodiment-conditioned learning to transfer human manipulation experience to robots.

A central test of Liber-0’s generalization is whether it can perform target tasks without robot demonstrations collected specifically for them. LiberAI evaluated the model on a separate suite of 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks, distinct from its internal scaling benchmarks: 20 pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, 20 non-PnP manipulation tasks, and 20 challenging non-PnP and long-horizon tasks.

Examples from the suite include placing a pen in a pencil case, pushing a drawer closed, and a longer sequence in which a pen is placed in a pouch and the pouch is stored in a drawer.

LiberAI reported task success rates of 63.5% on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on non-pick-and-place manipulation tasks and 10.5% on challenging non-pick-and-place and long-horizon tasks, with an overall success rate of 36.0% across 600 trials.

Here, zero-shot means the evaluated checkpoint was not trained on robot demonstrations collected specifically for these target tasks; pretraining still included robot data.

Why learn from people?

Robot manipulation has traditionally relied heavily on demonstrations recorded on a specific robot for a specific task, usually by a human operator teleoperating the machine. That data closely matches deployment, but collecting it can be slow and expensive, particularly when new tasks or robot platforms require additional demonstrations. Human activity is far more abundant, and much of it is already on video.

The obstacle, according to LiberAI, is that human video does not translate directly into robot commands. Cameras sit in different places, hand poses estimated from video are noisy, and human bodies move differently from robots.

Liber-0 connects human experience with robot action in three ways. First, LiberSense Glove, LiberAI’s data-collection system, directly records hand movements, helping link human video to the motions behind it. Second, LiberAI’s robot platform uses camera views and hand, wrist and waist movements that more closely match those of humans, making skills easier to transfer. Third, a Unified Embodiment Representation gives the model information about body shape and joint movement, so it can adapt actions to the body performing them.

Liber-0 jointly predicts future video frames and actions. This lets it learn from ordinary videos without action labels alongside glove and robot recordings that include measured motion.

Human-to-robot transfer. Conceptual illustration of how action-grounded human recordings and visual and kinematic alignment support transfer to LEO.

Learning actions that robot data lacked

Glove data can also introduce behaviors missing from a policy’s robot data. LiberAI trained policies whose robot demonstrations covered only pick-and-place, while glove demonstrations included actions such as folding, pressing and opening. Performance was measured as a progress score, a 0 to 100 measure that credits partial completion, across four pick-and-place and six non-PnP tasks. With robot data alone, the non-PnP progress score was 2.2. Adding glove recordings of those actions raised it to 47.5, and to 54.6 when the glove set also included pick-and-place, close to the 56.3 scored by a policy trained on robot demonstrations of every action. This controlled experiment is separate from the 60-task suite: the actions appeared in the glove demonstrations but not in the policies’ robot demonstrations.

A separate experiment examines whether glove recordings can reduce the need for robot demonstrations. In an eight-task evaluation on LiberAI’s robot platform, where the full robot and glove pools contained equal numbers of demonstrations, a policy trained on 25% of the robot pool plus 100% of the glove pool reached a progress score of 75.6. A policy trained on 100% of the robot pool scored 72.8.

In that setting, glove recordings delivered comparable performance with 75% fewer robot demonstrations. The saving applies to robot demonstrations specifically, as the mixed policy still drew on the full glove pool. Because glove collection does not require a robot at each site, LiberAI says experience can be gathered from more people, in more places, and potentially at lower cost.

On LiberAI’s internal benchmarks, the pretrained checkpoint achieved progress scores of 81.4 on pick-and-place and 72.3 on non-PnP tasks when evaluated directly. Robot post-training added 2.2 and 1.5 points, to 83.6 and 73.8. LiberAI said the small gain indicates the pretrained model already captures much of the capability needed for the evaluated tasks.

LiberAI has developed an interactive simulation in which users can upload their own objects and watch Liber-0 manipulate them in a virtual environment. The simulation demonstrates object-level generalization: that version of the model was post-trained on 100 hours of simulated teleoperation data and receives no further object-specific training.

“Human video shows what people do, but not exactly how their hands move or how that movement fits a different body,” said Songming Liu, founder and CEO of LiberAI. “Grounding that experience in measured motion and aligning it with the robot’s body is what turns it into robot capability.”

Wireless chargers are being deployed in a number of indoor and outdoor applications for charging the mobile robots. | Credit: WiBotic

As robot fleets scale, charging becomes an operational challenge. Understanding how to optimize charging for fleets of mobile robots is key to getting the best performance from the fleet throughout the day.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic

With growing deployments, charging is becoming more than a question of how long a battery lasts or how quickly it can recharge. Charging strategy can affect fleet uptime, facility infrastructure, maintenance requirements, and even the size of the batteries that robot manufacturers need to carry.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic, recently joined The Robot Report Podcast to discuss how those considerations are changing as robot fleets scale.

He also discussed opportunity charging, the tradeoffs around fast charging, WiBotic’s move toward higher-power systems, and how charging data could help operators identify power problems.

This is an excerpt from the podcast interview. Listen to the full audio anywhere you get your podcasts or online in the show notes.

WiBotic expands beyond its traditional robotics markets

What has changed recently at WiBotic, and how is the market maturing?

Waters: Overall, WiBotic has diversified into a few different markets, but all the while, robotics has really been growing, as we all know, over the last last one to two years for sure.

That was a big motivator for us to pursue getting into some adjacent markets. Take, for example, floor care, medical carts, space, and defense applications, all of which are markets that really use the same product as our longstanding robotics customers from a wireless charging, autonomous charging perspective.

Flash-forward a year of focusing on that and putting all the internal operational, sales, and engineering teams in place to support different markets. Here we are a year and a half later, and robotics is booming everywhere you look, right? I mean, all of our legacy customers in robotics have had significant volume growth this year.

We are seeing huge growth in automotive AMR adoption. We are seeing growth in outdoor robotic inspection for energy substations, and a lot of outdoor applications are growing. And then there’s the wild card of humanoids.

Wireless charging is a really interesting dynamic in humanoids as far as what it can enable and how it can improve uptime and eliminate some of these Achilles’ heels issues that humanoids have around downtime.

Opportunity charging changes the equation for large robot fleets

As fleets of mobile robots grow, where does charging start creating operational friction?

Waters: The big trend as charging relates to operational impact is what we’ve probably talked about before with Gene [Demaitre]. WiBotic has always looked at as a great opportunity for wireless charging. But, you know, it takes a while for fleets to get big enough for it to truly make sense. And I think we’re finally at that place. And what I’m referring to is opportunity charging.

So it’s the concept of “Don’t just put the chargers on the sides of the factories.” And then when the battery on the robot gets to 20%, that robot might be on the far side of the factory. Now it’s got to drive 10 minutes while watching out for everything else and while being ignored by the fleet management for doing a task, even though it’s in an area where a task needs to get done, right? Because it has to go charge.

That strategy, which is arguably easier to implement at a small scale, because you can truly just say, “If any one of these robots’ batteries hits 20%, stop and go drive to the charging station.” That’s fairly easy to implement. That gets really complicated, and that leads to a lot of unwanted downtime when the fleets start to get bigger. Even like fleets of 20 to 40, this becomes a bottleneck.

We need to implement opportunity charging. And it doesn’t make sense to do opportunity charging with anything but wireless. Because if you did it with contacts, your robots would be hitting the contacts so many more times. And even if you had the world’s most strongest contact, it still would require maintenance at some point, times all of the chargers in your fleet.

If the robot does a task and it’s got 10 seconds to sit there, well, a charging station should be positioned right where that robot naturally is going to sit.

You could look at that as well. It’s only charging for 10 seconds, but if you do that often enough, it’s adding substantial energy back into the batteries across the fleet and allowing these things to run 24/7.

You can completely eliminate that. Just allow the robots to stay in the loops where they’re operating when you employ opportunity charging. So that’s really the trend that we’ve been seeing and the demand we’ve been getting, and the main reason why companies are looking for wireless power.

Submit your innovation now!

Charging should be part of the robot design process

How should companies think about charging during system design instead of treating it as an accessory at the end?

Waters: If I boil it down to three things, I think companies should be thinking about power infrastructure. I’ll come back to a few details on these. Where are your electrical outlets, and how many of them do you have, and are they rated for enough power to handle all the chargers you want to deploy? So think about that up front. That bites people. We’ve seen a lot when you think about that too late.

I think people are really questioning. How big of a battery do I need? Do I need a battery that supports an eight-hour runtime? Do I need a battery that supports super fast charging? In the world of batteries, most of these types of things trade off with each other.

They might be overdesigning it. They might be adding way too much battery cost for what they really need, especially if they’re thinking about charging strategies.

We still hear a lot of customers be like, “We need to charge these things as fast as humanly possible.” And we’re going to listen, and we’re going to assume the customers made the right choices for the right reasons.

But sometimes, we do have a strong relationship with someone, we get into these topics. It’s not our job necessarily to push back, but we are curious battery guys, and we’re a friendly company to work with. So we sometimes ask: “Do you really want to charge at 3°C all the time? Have you seen a data sheet from the battery manufacturer that says what that’s gonna do to lifetime? Is that worth it?”

And then the third thing for sure is maintenance. If you wait till you’ve already finished your design, and you’re starting to deploy and haven’t thought about those things, then almost surely, you will get bit by every one of those things within at least a couple of months, if not sooner.

WiBotic develops chargers for outdoor robots, drones and humanoids

As WiBotic moves into new applications, how have its products evolved?

Waters: WiBotic has always really tried to think about what product serves the maximum number of customers and people, right? We’re not a consulting business where we customize every system.

As far as developing circuits and certifying systems, we want to be a company that makes standard products and sells systems to customers that they can depend on that are supported and certified.

We most recently launched in our 1 kW product family an IP65-rated version of the charger. When we first launched our 1 kW product a couple years ago, it was just available in our typical black box IP20 form factor.

So we now have an IP65 form factor, which is really needed for outdoor applications and robotics. Really desirable from, you know, indoor applications like floor care where water and dust are very much parts of those systems.

Right now, we are actively developing more around two areas of innovation. One is size and weight. We are seeing a lot of interest in drone applications. WiBotic certainly has had a long history with drones.

We’re developing lightweight, high-power systems for drones, which just so happens to be kind of the same thing that humanoids need as well.

The more mass you add to a humanoid, the more energy it has to spend because it’s balancing that mass. And there’s not a lot of space. So yeah, we’re focusing on a lot of small form-factor, high-power applications, as well as pushing the power of our current products up to a 3 kW level.

The new ISO 21423:2026 standard is intended to facilitate communications among different mobile robots. Source: mansyupasara AI, Adobe Stock

As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model.

“Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.”

“Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”

ISO 21423 addresses IMR interoperability

Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles (AGVs), autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility.

The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers, and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained.

For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning, which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.

Submit your innovation now!

Standard also covers communications with other systems

ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. People using or wearing mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots.

“ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in robotics standardization efforts,” said the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization. The standard is available at the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320.

The Association for Advancing Automation is a leading global advocate for the benefits of automating. Members of A3 represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, systems integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms.

A3 hosts events including the International Robot Safety Conference, the A3 Business Forum, and Automate.

Tutor trains its Sonny robot on real-world manipulation tasks. Credit: Eugene Demaitre

Real-world data, human “tutors,” and simulation are all part of the recipe for training AI models to enable next-generation robots to tackle a widening variety of tasks. Tutor Intelligence Inc. today said it has raised $75 million in Series B funding as it works toward general-purpose robotics.

“It’s not only that Tutor’s models let robots do jobs that robots have never been able to do before,” stated Josh Gruenstein, co-founder and CEO of Tutor Intelligence. “This type of intelligence also makes robots affordable on a whole new level. We’re unlocking much broader access to the solutions that businesses need to survive and that make basic goods cheaper for everybody. And the demand is there. We can hardly build robots fast enough.”

Tutor Intelligence spun out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (MIT CSAIL) in 2021. The Watertown, Mass.-based company asserted that it is building a full technology stack to “close the gap between what robots can do and what people can do.”

Data flywheel accelerates robot deployment

“Artificial intelligence has transformed the digital world, learning to converse and code from the internet’s vast record of text and images,” said Tutor Intelligence. “The physical world has no such record to train on, and AI has yet to transform it in the same way.”

The company has deployed fleets of internet-connected robots into production environments, where they do real work for customers with input from remote operators known as “tutors.” It uses the real-world data to train better frontier models, ultimately making the robots more capable.

Tutor claimed that its “full-stack platform” and “data flywheel” accelerate deployment, making robots more scalable, safer, and more affordable. Instead of a robots-as-a-service (RaaS) model, business pay Tutor by the hour or by the pick, the same way they pay for manual labor.

Customers make no upfront purchase and sign no long-term contract, added Tutor. The company said it handles deployment and maintenance and regularly sends software and intelligence upgrades. Tutor said its approach is bringing automation to tasks that have long defied conventional, deterministic robotics. It opened a “Data Factory” earlier this year to evaluate policies across 100 physical robots.

Submit your innovation now!

Tutor Intelligence gets traction with Sonny and Cassie

Tutor’s Data Factory includes the Sonny two-armed, semi-humanoid robots for each picking. Cassie is a mobile manipulator designed for case picking and palletizing.

The company reported that twice as many of its robots are working in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago. It said it is on track to have more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027, all of which will be built in and deployed from the U.S. (The tutors may be overseas.)

The robots are currently moving, lifting, and manipulating objects across some of the country’s largest manufacturing and logistics networks. They handle breakfast cereals, snacks, candy, cosmetics, home goods, toys, and more.

Tutor noted that its growth reflects maturing enterprise adoption of physical AI, as companies move from pilots to expectations of a return on investment from automating their operations. Nearly a third of organizations that received Tutor robots in the past 12 months were existing customers installing more robots, it said.

Funding to support more training and manufacturing

Andreessen Horowitz led Tutor Intelligence’s Series B round, which brings its total capital raised to $117 million. Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led the company’s Series A and seed rounds, respectively, also participated.

“Tutor’s insight is that deployment isn’t just the destination for robotics research—it’s how you overcome its limitations,” said Raghu Raghuram, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz and former CEO of VMware.

“Rather than asking the real world to fit the research, Tutor starts with what real-world deployments demand and works backward through distribution, hardware and research,” he added. “Continual learning across an expanding range of deployments is the path from specialized capabilities to general-purpose robotics.”

Tutor said its latest investment its frontier robot foundation model training, as well as manufacturing and deployment of Sonny and Cassie. It announced the latest models of its robots and underlying platform last month.

]]> Portuguese DefenceTech scale-up TEKEVER has today announced that they have secured €13 million from EIFO as part of their Series D raise of €520 million ($580 million) at a €5.7 billion ($6.4 billion) valuation to support the company’s continued growth.

The first close was announced on 23 September 2026. This puts TEKEVER close to Denmark’s ecosystem for drones, robotics, testing and research, creating new opportunities for collaboration with Danish companies and research institutions.

Ricardo Mendes, CEO of TEKEVER, says: “EIFO’s commitment to join the second close of our Series D is a meaningful step in TEKEVER’s long-term engagement with Denmark and the Nordic region. The Nordic countries are vital to Europe’s sovereignty and resilience.

In Portugal, Lisbon-based Beyond Vision raised over €28 million to expand AI-powered drone production, while Germany’s Quantum Systems secured a €1 billion Series D to scale its unmanned systems.

Overall, EU-Startups has seen around €1.07 billion in adjacent funding in 2026, rising to roughly €1.59 billion including TEKEVER’s reported €520 million Series D.

“Europe needs defence companies that can grow and deliver at scale. TEKEVER has already demonstrated its ability to turn advanced technology into operational solutions. With this investment, we are supporting the company’s next phase of growth while also bringing a tangible TEKEVER presence to Denmark,” adds Peder Lundquist, CEO of EIFO.

Founded in 2001 in Lisbon, TEKEVER is an IT, aerospace, defense, and security company that develops AI-powered autonomous drone systems for applications including surveillance and intelligence gathering

TEKEVER’s drone systems have reportedly completed more than 50,000 operational flight hours in Ukraine, and the company has secured long-term defence programmes in countries including Germany, the United Kingdom and Portugal.

Through today’s announcement, the company is now set to establish its first operational presence in the Nordics and in Denmark.

As supply chains become increasingly strategic to our customers, they are looking for solutions that improve productivity, flexibility and resilience. With today’s acquisition of Logiqs we add another core technology that, over time, will bring roaming pallet AS/RS capabilities to the AutoStore platform, helping us address a broader set of needs for both new and existing customers,” said Mats Hovland Vikse, CEO of AutoStore.

Based in the Netherlands, Logiqs develops roaming robots for the automated storage and retrieval of palletised goods. Its warehouse technology is deployed at about 30 customer sites across multiple geographies and end markets, helping customers improve storage density, throughput, and operational efficiency. 

The company also offers greenhouse automation and vertical farming systems. Logiqs’ 60 employees bring complementary automation, software and product capabilities to AutoStore.

]]> According to McKinsey’s 2026 Quantum Technology Monitor, investment in quantum technology startups reached €11.15 billion ($12.6 billion) in 2025, 6.3 times more than a year earlier. Only 3% came from public sources, including governments, sovereign wealth funds and universities. In 2024, their share had been roughly one-third.

That can look odd next to the size of the quantum programmes being announced by governments. The numbers are describing different things. Public commitments can pay for laboratories, university research, testbeds, training and infrastructure. The capital that goes onto a startup’s balance sheet comes from a different mix of sources.

When I look at the funding picture, I separate money that builds the ecosystem from money that finances the company. European quantum founders need both, but one does not automatically provide the other.

Europe starts with a strong research base

Europe does not lack quantum research capacity. The MIT Quantum Index estimates that the EU produces 22% of global quantum-computing publications and 17% of the top 10% most-cited papers in the field. The UK and Germany each account for 6% of those highly cited papers.

The training base is expanding as well. The same report counted 69 master’s degrees worldwide with “quantum” in the degree name. Germany had 12, the highest number of any country, and the UK had 10.

Public programmes support much of the environment around that research: universities, laboratories, shared infrastructure and training. A company can benefit from all of it without receiving the programme’s money as equity. A national quantum commitment may improve the conditions for building a startup while financing very little of the startup itself.

Public money and startup money do different jobs

The 2025 funding data makes the split visible. Investment in quantum technology startups rose sharply, while the share coming from public sources fell to 3% from roughly one-third a year earlier.

Public support still underpins the sector, but company financing increasingly comes through other channels. Venture and private equity investors, corporates, and public markets supplied most of the capital going directly into quantum companies.

For a founder, the useful question is not simply how much a government has committed to quantum. It is where the money is intended to go. A programme may support university research, shared infrastructure, workforce development or direct company funding. These routes can all strengthen the same ecosystem, but they do not create the same financing options for a startup.

Read the programme before counting the capital

Large national commitments are often reported as evidence of how much capital is moving into quantum. For a company building its financing plan, the headline amount is not enough.

I would look first at how the programme is allocated and who can receive the money. Funding directed to national laboratories or universities can strengthen the technology base without appearing on a startup’s balance sheet. Investment in infrastructure or training may reduce barriers for companies across the ecosystem, but it is different from capital that a founder can use to finance the business directly.

This does not make those programmes less valuable. Quantum companies need the research base, specialist talent and infrastructure they help create. The distinction becomes important only when founders start treating ecosystem funding as a measure of how much company financing is available.

The same logic applies when comparing countries. A large public commitment can make one market a better place to develop quantum technology without necessarily making it easier to raise the private capital required to scale a company.

The financing plan still has to extend beyond the research base

Quantum companies can spend years moving from research towards systems that are ready for wider commercial use. The funding environment changes during that journey.

The sources of capital flowing into quantum companies have already shifted. Venture and private equity remain important, but corporate and public-market capital have also become significant parts of the sector’s financing.

European founders do not need to predict every source of future capital at the beginning. They do need to know which parts of the development plan are covered by the money already available and which are not.

That is particularly relevant in Europe. Research, training and public infrastructure are genuine advantages. They can make it easier to start a quantum company and develop the underlying technology. They do not remove the need to finance the company itself as it moves towards commercial scale.

The sector is attracting far more capital than it did only a few years ago. For European founders, the useful question is not whether money is flowing into quantum. It is which part of that money can reach their company, what it can fund and what they will need after it runs out.

]]> Alethio Therapeutics (Alethio), an Abingdon-on-Thames-based biopharmaceutical company developing next-generation therapies for myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), has announced the completion of an oversubscribed €80.46 million ($90 million/£67 million) Series A financing.

The round was co-led by new investors Sofinnova Partners and RA Capital, alongside founding investor Oxford Science Enterprises, with additional support from Cancer Research Horizons and the University of Oxford. As part of the financing, Graziano Seghezzi, Managing Partner at Sofinnova Partners, and Maxwell DeNies of RA Capital have joined Alethio’s Board of Directors.

“The most transformative companies are built around insights that challenge long-held assumptions in medicine. In MPNs, the field has long accepted that controlling the disease is enough. Alethio challenges that assumption. By targeting the cells that drive the disease, its approach has the potential to move patients beyond symptom management toward true disease modification. All of this is based on an exceptional team and founders with a deep understanding of the disease,” said Graziano Seghezzi, Managing Partner at Sofinnova Partners.

Alethio was founded in 2021 as a spin-out from the University of Oxford by Professors Adam Mead and Beth Psaila, two globally recognised physician-scientists in MPNs. Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), including essential thrombocythaemia (ET), are blood cancers characterised by the uncontrolled production of blood cells and an increased risk of thrombosis, bone marrow scarring (myelofibrosis), and transformation to acute leukaemia, the UK startup explained. 

“Alethio Therapeutics was born from years of research at the University of Oxford and from our direct experience treating patients with MPNs. We founded the company to ensure that deep human disease insight and rigorous science translate into medicines that can alter disease progression, not just manage its symptoms. Our aim is to offer patients real hope — helping them live longer, healthier lives,” co-founders Mead and Psaila mentioned on the website. 

According to the company, current therapies for ET are non-targeted treatments that have been around for decades, such as hydroxycarbamide and interferon, that can affect, and disproportionately damage, healthy cells. 

Alethio claims to be pursuing a different approach, developing targeted therapies designed to selectively eliminate the disease-driving cells that sustain MPNs. The company notes that this approach modifies the underlying disease features, restores healthy blood counts, reduces thrombotic risk, and ultimately improves patient outcomes.

“Too often, a patient’s first encounter with ET is a thrombotic event that lands them in the emergency room. What follows is typically lifelong treatment with therapies that can cause burdensome side effects and are associated with high rates of resistance. Alethio was founded on a simple conviction – if you can selectively eliminate the cells driving disease, you can redefine what is possible for patients. This financing enables us to turn that conviction into reality,” said Dr. Rohit Batta, Chief Executive Officer of Alethio Therapeutics.

Alethio’s lead programme, ATX-011, is a first-in-class monoclonal antibody that targets G6B, designed to treat essential thrombocythaemia. G6B is a novel target in MPN, uniquely expressed on MPN-initiating stem cells but not on healthy stem cells. It is also expressed on megakaryocytes and platelets — the cells that drive thrombosis and transformation to myelofibrosis.

The UK startup highlighted that these findings support ATX-011’s potential to deliver broad therapeutic benefit across patients with MPNs, regardless of driver mutation. Alethio is advancing ATX-011 through IND-enabling studies and toward clinical development in ET.

It also reported that preclinical data for ATX-011 has been selected for oral presentation at the American Society of Hematology (ASH) 2026 Annual Meeting. 

The company has also built ARTEMIS (Advanced Research & Translational Engine for Myeloproliferative Neoplasms), which is an integrated discovery and development engine for MPNs. Alethio says ARTEMIS is designed to systematically identify, validate, and de-risk novel mutant drivers of disease and therapeutic candidates against these targets.

Powered by ARTEMIS, Alethio is building a pipeline of novel biologic disease-modifying therapies for MPNs. Alongside ATX-011, it is also developing a programme targeting mutant calreticulin (CALR)–driven disease, which occurs in roughly 30% of patients with MPNs.

“Since its formation, Alethio has made incredible progress in translating pioneering University of Oxford science into a focused and ambitious biotechnology company. The team has built not only a promising lead programme but also the ARTEMIS discovery platform, providing a powerful engine for future pipeline innovation. We are proud to continue supporting the company and are delighted to welcome such an experienced syndicate to help Alethio transition to the next stage of growth; delivering meaningful impact for patients in the clinic,” said Sally Dewhurst, Principal at Oxford Science Enterprises. 

The company plans to use this capital to transition into a clinical-stage company, deploying capital to advance its lead programme, ATX-011, through completion of Phase 1/2a studies in essential thrombocythaemia (ET) and to Phase 3 readiness, while also progressing additional MPN programmes toward IND submission.

The round also saw continued participation from investors Grid.vc and Harjavalta Ventures. Vensum Power had raised €3.8 million Seed funding in 2023, and the Series A round brings its total funding to €15.2 million since its founding in 2018.

“Data centres are competing with every other sector for the same grid capacity, and Vensum Power tackles one of the most overlooked inefficiencies in the system: converting power into a form that equipment can use optimally,” said Prashant Chiranjive Jain, Managing Director of L&T Vyoma and Head of L&T Electronic Products & Systems, both business verticals of Larsen & Toubro.

Vensum Power was founded in 2018 and currently employs around 20 people. It develops power conversion technology that it describes as near-lossless. While conventional power converters are engineered around a narrow peak-efficiency point and typically require redesign for each new application, Vensum’s product is designed to deliver high efficiency across fluctuating loads.

Vensum Power says its converters are among the world’s smallest at their power class, and engineered for use across AI data centres, EV charging stations, energy storage systems, renewable energy installations, and DC microgrids.

As electricity demand surges, driven by global electrification and AI infrastructure buildout, efficient power conversion has moved from a technical necessity to a foundational strategic need. Vensum Power is pitching its ability to deliver near-lossless power conversion as a critical advantage in environments like AI data centres, where workloads change rapidly, and every watt lost to heat must also be cooled.

The Finnish DeepTech company says it will use the fresh capital to scale its product from development to industrial-scale delivery. The company’s Software-Defined Power Conversion platform, which uses soft-switching techniques and digital control to minimise energy losses, is set to enter mass production at partner factories in 2027.

Initial products, Vensum Power says, will serve EV charging and energy storage markets, with AI data centres to follow as the next main target.

“The funding round propels us from developing technology to delivering it at industrial scale and bringing the same proven solution to AI data centres, where access to power has become the main bottleneck. The question in data centres is no longer only how powerful the chips are, but how efficiently the used electricity actually reaches them. Thanks to the software-defined approach, our converters operate consistently at extremely high efficiency even with rapidly changing loads,” said Peter Nisula, CEO of Vensum Power.

Near-lossless energy conversion has been one of the biggest challenges in the power sector; Vensum Power is advancing closer to that goal with its first products for EV charging and energy storage entering mass production. As Nisula noted, the critical question for AI data centres is not how powerful the chips are, but how efficiently the electricity actually reaches them, and if Vensum’s SDPC platform solves that at industrial scale, a problem the company is now moving to solve at scale.

]]> The European Commission has adopted the 2027 European Innovation Council (EIC) Work Programme, allocating €1.8 billion to support DeepTech startups, scale-ups and researchers across Europe.

The funding package aims to help promising technologies move from early-stage research to commercialisation, while improving access to investment for women-led and DefenceTech companies.

Ekaterina Zaharieva, Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, says: “This is how it puts our Startup and Scaleup Strategy into action: mobilising more capital, stimulating customer deals, cutting complexity, and making bold investments on the technologies that will shape our future. And, as we shape the next EU research and innovation programme, our task is to turn Europe’s scientific excellence, talent and industrial strength into new companies and lasting competitiveness.”

The programme marks the final EIC funding package under Horizon Europe 2021–2027, the EU’s research and innovation framework.

A significant part of the programme focuses on expanding access to growth capital. This includes completing the €1 billion commitment to the Scaleup Europe Fund, launched in 2026 and managed by investment firm EQT. The fund aims to attract at least €4 billion from other investors and support European technology companies through investments averaging more than €100 million.

Alongside this initiative, the EIC will continue supporting startups through its STEP Scale Up scheme, targeting companies developing strategic technologies. The 2027 programme also completes funding allocations of €200 million for defence investments and €25 million for the Advanced Innovation Challenges pilot, both introduced in 2026.

These measures form part of the EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy and the Competitiveness Compass, two initiatives intended to strengthen Europe’s innovation ecosystem and address obstacles faced by technology companies seeking to grow.

Established under Horizon Europe in 2021, the EIC has a budget exceeding €10 billion for the 2021–2027 period. Since its launch, it has supported more than 800 companies and nearly 700 research projects, providing financial assistance at different stages of technological development.

Its investment arm, the EIC Fund, has already invested close to €2 billion in more than 375 deep tech startups, attracting approximately 3.5 times that amount in co-investment.

The programme also expands support for women-led startups through a redesigned Women TechEU initiative, doubling individual grants to €150k. A new European Prize for Women Innovators in Quantum will also be introduced, complementing the existing European Prize for Women Innovators and recognising female entrepreneurs working in quantum technologies.

Another priority is helping EIC-backed startups secure their first customers. New measures will connect companies with public and private procurers, allowing them to test emerging technologies and explore potential commercial applications.

Support for dual-use and defence technologies will remain part of the EIC’s activities, reflecting the EU’s interest in strengthening its technological capabilities across strategic sectors.

At the same time, the Commission intends to reduce administrative complexity and make funding more accessible to innovators at different stages of development.

]]> Munich-based aviation startup VÆRIDION has raised €30 million in a Series A2 funding round and selected for a €94.5 million grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund, bringing the combined value to €124.5 million.

The investment round was co-led by Dutch investors SHIFT Invest and Invest-NL, with participation from existing backers World Fund, Project A and Vsquared Ventures. PAYBACK founder and DeepTech investor Alexander Rittweger also joined the round. VÆRIDION has raised approximately €60 million to date, excluding the newly announced EU grant.

Ivor van Dartel, founder and CEO of VÆRIDION, says: “Over the past year, we have turned the Microliner from a validated design into hardware, with exceptional capital efficiency. Our propulsion and battery technology is now being tested at our own facility in Oberpfaffenhofen. This equity round enables us to build our first conforming aircraft. The Commission’s selection of CAROLUS supports the next step: establishing the industrial capability for Microliner production.

“Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide.”

VÆRIDION’s announcement comes amid other European funding rounds for next-generation aircraft and aerospace technologies in 2026.

In France, AURA AERO announced a €50 million Series B to advance its electric and hybrid-electric aircraft programmes, while HyLight raised €13 million for hydrogen-powered autonomous airships. In the UK, Greenjets secured €35 million for aerospace propulsion technology and Skyfly raised €8.91 million for electric aircraft development.

Elsewhere, Denmark’s Acodyne secured €2.5 million for unmanned cargo aircraft, while Germany’s SPREAD AI raised €25 million for industrial engineering software serving sectors including aerospace.

Together with VÆRIDION’s €30 million equity round, these selected announcements represent approximately €164.4 million in financing, excluding VÆRIDION’s separately selected EU grant.

EU-Startups previously covered VÆRIDION’s €14 million Series A in December 2024, led by returning investor World Fund.

Daria Saharova, Managing Partner at World Fund, adds: “For the past half century, Airbus has shown that Europe can build aircraft the world buys. VÆRIDION is writing the next chapter with a fully electric aircraft, built in Bavaria, with a clear path to certification. Investing in the future of aviation is Europe’s power play, and I am proud to back Ivor and the team.”

Founded in 2021 by former Airbus manager Ivor van Dartel and headquartered in Munich, VÆRIDION is developing fully electric aircraft designed to make short-distance regional aviation more economically viable.

Its flagship aircraft, the Microliner, aims to carry nine passengers over distances of approximately 400 kilometres, connecting regional destinations that have become increasingly difficult to serve profitably using conventional aircraft.

The €30 million investment will finance the development of VÆRIDION’s first certification-conforming aircraft and further propulsion testing. Meanwhile, the €94.5 million Innovation Fund grant is intended to support the CAROLUS project, which will establish and scale up a final assembly facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, near Munich.

The project was selected from 358 applications as one of 12 large-scale projects, making VÆRIDION the only German company and the only aviation project selected in this category. The grant remains subject to the completion of an agreement expected in 2027.

The Microliner combines a glider-inspired wing with patented modular battery technology and a multi-engine propulsion system driving a single propeller. It is being developed in passenger and cargo configurations, with a targeted range of 400 kilometres carrying nine passengers under Instrument Flight Rules, or up to 550 kilometres carrying four passengers under Visual Flight Rules.

The company is targeting operating costs below €0.40 per seat-kilometre, which it believes could allow operators to offer tickets at prices comparable to first-class journeys on Germany’s ICE high-speed trains. Its broader ambition is to restore regional connections, including services linking smaller German cities and airfields that are no longer served by commercial airlines.

Thijs Gitmans, General Partner at SHIFT Invest, adds: “Regional aviation is one of the clearest cases where electrification makes both environmental and commercial sense. VÆRIDION has chosen a certification pathway regulators already understand and has delivered real hardware on a disciplined budget. We are proud to lead this round and to back a European champion in electric flight with European funding.”

The company reports customer commitments for more than 130 aircraft, representing a potential value exceeding €730 million. Its launch customer is Belgium-based ASL Group, with the first Microliner delivery targeted for 2030.

In March 2026, VÆRIDION opened its production and testing facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, where it has since powered on its electric engine for the first time. The facility was acquired following the insolvency of German electric aviation startup Lilium.

The startup is now preparing to integrate its battery packs and propulsion system into a ground-testing platform known as a copper bird. Alongside wind-tunnel testing, this work will support the development of its first certification-conforming prototype, currently targeted for late 2027 or early 2028.

With engineering activities in Munich and Delft, and production planned in Bavaria, VÆRIDION intends to expand its European team as it progresses towards flight testing, certification and industrial production.

Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Aviation experts explain what happens https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/can-planes-fall-out-sky Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:57:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55522 Aircraft are engineered to withstand extraordinary forces, but the physics of flight leave little room for error. Here we examine the mechanics behind aerodynamic stalls, severe icing, loss of control and structural failure, exploring the factors that can turn a routine flight into a battle to stay airborne.

The post Can planes really fall out of the sky? Aviation experts explain what happens appeared first on AGN.

]]> The idea of an aircraft suddenly dropping out of the sky is frankly terrifying. Yet while it makes for a dramatic headline, the reality is considerably more complicated – and thankfully exceptionally unusual.

Aircraft are designed with multiple layers of protection against losing control, but under certain circumstances, a combination of aerodynamic forces, weather and mechanical problems can overwhelm even the most sophisticated aircraft.

The tragic Learjet 60 crash in Florida recently is a sobering reminder of how quickly things can go wrong. The aircraft, which was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard.

In communications with air traffic control shortly before the accident, the crew reported icing, moderate turbulence and deteriorating weather conditions, followed by an extremely rapid descent.

According to preliminary statements from NTSB investigators, there is evidence the aircraft may have begun breaking up before impact, although the circumstances remain under investigation

It is too early to draw conclusions about what happened. However, the circumstances raise a wider question around what actually causes an aircraft to lose altitude so dramatically.

What causes an aircraft to come down?

Among the many reasons an aircraft can lose altitude rapidly is an aerodynamic stall. Investigators have not indicated whether a stall played any role in the Florida accident, but the event has prompted renewed interest in how stalls occur and why they can be dangerous.

Despite the popular association with engine failure, a stall has nothing directly to do with an engine stopping.

It occurs when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack, causing airflow to separate from the wing surface and lift to reduce sharply. The aircraft may pitch down, roll or enter an uncontrolled descent.

Stalls can happen at almost any speed if the angle of attack becomes high enough.

Ice makes this even more dangerous. Even a relatively small accumulation on a wing can disrupt the airflow, reducing lift while increasing drag. It can also change the aircraft’s stall characteristics, sometimes leaving pilots with less warning than they would normally expect.

Serving airline Captain and aviation safety specialist Pete Wilson told us:

“An aircraft can fall out of the sky for numerous reasons. It could be structural failure, such as part of the airframe breaking away, a control surface malfunction, for example a rudder failure, or a problem with the trim system. It could also be a loss of control caused by aerodynamic conditions such as ice, thunderstorms, severe turbulence or wind shear.”

He added:

“Another possibility is cargo shifting during flight. A good example is the Boeing 747 crash at Bagram, Afghanistan, in 2013, when an unsecured military vehicle shifted towards the rear of the aircraft shortly after take-off, damaging critical systems and leaving the pilots unable to control the aircraft. Not every failure is engine-related.”

Can an aircraft break apart during a rapid descent?

An aircraft descending rapidly can accelerate beyond its operating limits, known as overspeed condition. The resulting aerodynamic loads can become severe, potentially exceeding the structural limits of the airframe. In extreme circumstances, components or entire sections of the aircraft can separate.

Importantly, a steep descent does not necessarily mean an aircraft has suffered a structural failure. A jet can lose thousands of feet per minute while remaining largely intact.

Equally, what looks like an aircraft falling straight down may actually be the final result of it losing control earlier in the flight.

Florida Learjet crash: NTSB probes evidence aircraft broke up before impact Florida Learjet crash: NTSB probes evidence aircraft broke up before impact

Why engine failure does not necessarily mean a crash

An engine failure on its own is unlikely to make an aircraft suddenly lose height and crash. Most multi-engine aircraft can remain controllable following the loss of an engine, while even a complete loss of thrust does not mean an aircraft immediately stops flying.

Aircraft can glide, sometimes over considerable distances, depending on altitude, speed and configuration.

Aircraft accidents are rarely down to a single failure

It’s extremely rare for an aircraft to go from flying normally to falling out of control in an instant. Usually, a series of things goes wrong, sometimes within seconds, until the pilots can no longer keep the aircraft stabilised.

This is why accident investigations are so important. Investigators need to work out not just what happened at the end, but what led up to it, how different problems may have affected the aircraft and why safety systems were unable to prevent the crash.

]]> Why airlines abandoned the upper deck lounge era https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/why-airlines-abandoned-upper-deck-lounges/ Sat, 07 Nov 2026 11:49:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55546 There was a time when using the upper deck spaces on Boeing 747s for lounges and cocktail bars became the norm for long-haul premium travellers.

The post Why airlines abandoned the upper deck lounge era appeared first on AGN.

]]> For a brief period in aviation history, flying was about more than simply getting from one destination to another. On some of the world’s most luxurious aircraft, passengers could leave their seats, head upstairs and enjoy a drink in an exclusive lounge thousands of feet above the ground.

The upper-deck lounge became one of the most memorable features of the golden age of commercial aviation. From elegant cocktail bars to spacious social areas, these spaces represented an era when airlines competed to make the journey itself an experience.

Yet today, such lounges are almost entirely a thing of the past. So what happened to this distinctive feature of air travel?

The golden age of onboard lounges

The introduction of large, wide-bodied aircraft during the late 1960s transformed commercial aviation. Among the most important was the Boeing 747, which entered airline service in 1970.

Its distinctive hump-backed design created an opportunity that airlines were quick to exploit. The upper deck, initially relatively small, could be transformed into an exclusive passenger space.

Airlines including Pan Am, American Airlines and other international carriers experimented with upstairs lounges, cocktail bars and social areas. Some featured comfortable armchairs, tables, elegant lighting and even piano-style entertainment.

For premium passengers, these spaces offered something that conventional aircraft cabins could not: the freedom to get up, socialise and enjoy a drink away from their seats. The upper deck became a powerful marketing tool, helping airlines distinguish themselves in an increasingly competitive international travel market.

The Boeing 747 made it possible

Although the 747 was primarily designed to carry large numbers of passengers, its unusual upper-deck configuration gave airlines considerable flexibility.

Early versions featured a relatively short upper deck, leaving room for a staircase connecting the main cabin to the lounge above. The space was particularly attractive to first-class passengers, who could enjoy a more exclusive environment during long-haul flights.

However, not every airline used the area in the same way. Some installed dedicated bars, while others opted for smaller lounges or additional seating.

As the 747 evolved, the upper deck was gradually extended on later versions (-300, -400, -8I), allowing airlines to accommodate more passengers in business and first class. This marked the beginning of the end for the traditional upstairs lounge.

Economics began to outweigh luxury

One of the biggest reasons airlines abandoned onboard lounges was financial. Every square metre of an aircraft cabin represents potential revenue. A lounge containing comfortable seating, a bar and social space could accommodate far fewer paying passengers than a conventional seating arrangement.

As airlines became increasingly focused on profitability, dedicating valuable cabin space to passengers who might only use it occasionally became difficult to justify. The economics became even more challenging as premium cabins evolved.

Airlines discovered that passengers were often willing to pay considerably more for private suites, fully flat beds and enhanced personal service.

Rather than providing a shared social space, carriers could generate additional revenue by installing more premium seats. The lounge was increasingly viewed as an expensive luxury rather than a profitable investment.

Changing passenger expectations

Passenger expectations also changed significantly. During the early decades of commercial jet travel, flying was often considered a special occasion. Passengers dressed formally, enjoyed elaborate meals and appreciated the opportunity to socialise during long journeys.

Modern air travel is considerably different nowadays. Business travellers increasingly prioritise privacy, comfort and the ability to work during flights. Leisure passengers, meanwhile, often value entertainment systems, personal space and comfortable seating.

The introduction of individual entertainment screens, improved connectivity and increasingly sophisticated premium cabins reduced the appeal of communal lounges. Today’s business-class passenger may prefer a private suite with a lie-flat bed over a shared cocktail bar.

Safety and operational considerations

Safety and operational requirements also played a role. Aircraft interiors must comply with strict regulations covering emergency evacuation, passenger movement, and cabin safety.

Dedicated lounges add challenges, especially when passengers move during turbulence or the aircraft encounters unexpected conditions. Open social spaces also require careful consideration of passenger circulation and crew responsibilities.

Although lounges were not inherently unsafe, their operational demands added another layer of complexity for airlines already seeking to simplify cabin layouts.

The rise of airport lounges

Another important development was the growing popularity of premium airport lounges. Airlines increasingly invested in luxurious ground facilities where passengers could enjoy restaurant-quality food, comfortable seating, showers, bars and business facilities before boarding. These lounges offered several advantages over their airborne counterparts.

They were larger, easier to maintain and could accommodate passengers from multiple flights. They also allowed airlines to provide a premium experience without sacrificing valuable aircraft cabin space.

For many travellers, the airport lounge became the place to relax and socialise, while the aircraft itself became a more functional environment focused on reaching the destination comfortably.

Could upper-deck lounges ever return?

Although traditional upper-deck cocktail bars have largely disappeared, the idea of creating distinctive social spaces onboard aircraft has never completely vanished. Some modern airlines (such as Virgin Atlantic) have introduced onboard bars and dedicated social areas, particularly on long-haul aircraft such as the Airbus A380.

Emirates, for example, is well known for its first-class and business-class onboard lounge and bar on the A380, while other carriers have experimented with communal spaces and premium cabin features.

These modern interpretations demonstrate that passengers still appreciate the opportunity to move around and socialise during long flights. However, they are generally more compact and carefully integrated into the cabin design than the elaborate lounges of aviation’s earlier decades.

An aviation luxury that belongs to another era

The disappearance of the upper-deck lounge reflects a much wider transformation in commercial aviation.

Airlines have moved away from the idea that luxury necessarily means grand communal spaces, elaborate entertainment and extravagant onboard facilities. Instead, modern premium travel increasingly revolves around privacy, personal space and individual comfort.

The upper-deck lounge remains one of the most fascinating reminders of an era when airlines were prepared to sacrifice passenger capacity in pursuit of an unforgettable flying experience.

While a handful of modern aircraft still offer onboard social spaces, the golden age of the airborne cocktail lounge is unlikely to return in its original form.

For aviation enthusiasts, however, those upstairs bars and elegant lounges will always represent a time when flying was as much about the journey as the destination.
